eye.title: Eye Anatomy
eye.descriptor: Layers of the Eyeball, Lens, Retina, Tear Film & Eye Movements
eye.intro: The eye is a fluid-filled globe set deep in the bony orbit, with only about a sixth of its surface exposed to the air. Its clear front window, the cornea, and the adjustable lens behind it focus light onto the retina, a sheet of nervous tissue at the back of the eye that converts the image into electrical signals carried by the optic nerve to the brain.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: In the orbit; only about one-sixth of the eyeball is exposed, the rest protected by bone and the eyelids

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: Three layers: fibrous tunic (sclera and cornea), vascular tunic (choroid, ciliary body, iris) and the retina

keyFacts.label: Focusing
keyFacts.value: The cornea does most of the bending of light; the lens fine-tunes focus as the ciliary muscle changes its shape

keyFacts.label: Light control
keyFacts.value: The iris constricts the pupil in bright light and dilates it in dim light

keyFacts.label: Photoreceptors
keyFacts.value: Rods for low light; cones for daylight and colour vision

keyFacts.label: Tears
keyFacts.value: Spread by blinking and drained through the lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct into the nose

keyFacts.label: Movement
keyFacts.value: Extraocular muscles turn the eyeball; the medial and lateral recti move it side to side

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: Acuity chart, refraction, slit lamp, dilated fundus examination, tonometry, visual fields, OCT

sections.heading: Location, orbit and eyelids
sections.body: The eyeball sits in the orbit, a cone-shaped bony socket that shields all but about one-sixth of its surface. The exposed front is covered by the eyelids, which protect the eye, spread tears across its surface with each blink and limit how much light enters. Each lid is stiffened by a tarsal plate, and the upper lid is lifted by the levator muscle helped by a small smooth muscle, the superior tarsal (Müller) muscle, which is routinely involved in surgery for a drooping lid (ptosis). The lacrimal gland in the upper outer corner of the orbit produces the watery part of the tear film. Tears flow to the inner corner, collect in the lacrimal lake and pass through tiny canaliculi into the lacrimal sac and down the nasolacrimal duct into the nose, which is why crying makes the nose run. Blinking, driven by muscles supplied by cranial nerves III and VII, is the main pump for this drainage.

sections.heading: The three layers of the eyeball
sections.body: The wall of the eyeball has three coats. The outer fibrous tunic is the tough white sclera, continuous in front with the transparent cornea, which covers the anterior tip of the eye and lets light in; the cornea has five layers (epithelium, Bowman's membrane, stroma, Descemet's membrane and endothelium) and no blood vessels, which keeps it clear. The middle vascular tunic consists of the choroid, a pigmented, blood-rich layer lining the back of the eye; the ciliary body, a band just behind the corneoscleral junction (limbus) containing the ciliary muscle and ciliary processes; and the iris, the coloured smooth-muscle diaphragm whose central opening is the pupil. The innermost neural tunic is the retina, the nervous tissue that detects light. In front of the lens lies watery aqueous humour; the large cavity behind it holds the jelly-like vitreous body, which keeps the globe's shape.

sections.heading: Focusing light: cornea, lens and iris
sections.body: Light passes first through the dome-shaped cornea, which bends it strongly; most of the eye's focusing power comes from this air-cornea interface. The pupil then regulates how much light continues inward: the iris constricts it in bright light and dilates it in dim light. Behind the pupil the lens works with the cornea to bring the image to a sharp focus on the retina. The lens is held in place by suspensory ligaments (zonule fibres) attached to the ciliary body, and when the ciliary muscle contracts or relaxes it changes the shape of the lens and so its focal distance, a process called accommodation that lets objects at different distances stay sharp. If the optical power of the cornea and lens does not match the length of the eye the image is blurred; in short-sightedness (myopia), for example, the image is focused in front of the retina rather than on it.

sections.heading: The retina and the optic nerve
sections.body: When light reaches the retina, specialised photoreceptor cells turn it into electrical signals. Rods work in low light; cones work in daylight, provide colour and fine detail, and are concentrated at the fovea, the small central pit used for reading and recognising faces. The signals pass through layers of retinal nerve cells and leave the eye in the optic nerve, which carries them to the brain, where they become the images we see. The point where the nerve leaves is the optic disc, which has no photoreceptors and forms the blind spot. The inner retina is supplied by the central retinal artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery; the outer retina and optic nerve head by the choroidal circulation (short posterior ciliary arteries); and the ciliary body by the long posterior and anterior ciliary arteries. These vessels can be seen through the pupil with an ophthalmoscope, making the eye the one place where small arteries and veins can be inspected directly.

sections.heading: Muscles and nerves of the eye
sections.body: Three groups of muscles serve the eye. The six extraocular muscles turn the eyeball: the medial rectus pulls it inwards (adduction) and works in opposition to the lateral rectus, which pulls it outwards, while the superior and inferior recti and the two oblique muscles move it up, down and in rotation. The superior oblique is unusual in that its tendon passes through a fibrous pulley, the trochlea, before attaching to the eye, so it turns the eye down and out and rotates it inwards. The intraocular muscles, the iris sphincter and dilator and the ciliary muscle, control the size of the pupil and accommodation and are driven by the autonomic nervous system. The eyelid protractors and retractors open and close the lids. Sensation from the cornea is exquisitely sharp, which is why a speck of dust is so painful and why the blink reflex protects the eye so quickly.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance and investigation
sections.body: Each layer has its own disorders: corneal scratches and infections, clouding of the lens (cataract), raised pressure damaging the optic nerve (glaucoma), and retinal disease from diabetes, high blood pressure or age-related degeneration. Visual acuity is measured by reading progressively smaller letters on a chart, and refraction uses a series of lenses to find the correction that makes them sharpest. A slit lamp, a microscope with a thin beam of light, shows the cornea, iris and lens. Dilating drops allow the fundus (retina, vessels and optic nerve head) to be viewed with an ophthalmoscope, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) images the retinal layers in cross-section. Tonometry measures the eye pressure. Visual field testing maps side vision, and electrical tests (ERG and VEP) record the responses of the photoreceptors and optic nerves.

larynx.title: Larynx Anatomy
larynx.descriptor: Cartilages, Vocal Folds, Muscles & the Voice
larynx.intro: The larynx, or voice box, is a cartilaginous segment of the airway in the front of the neck, suspended from the hyoid bone above and continuous with the trachea below. Its first job is to guard the lower airway, closing off the trachea so that food and drink cannot be inhaled; its second is phonation, the production of sound by the vocal folds.

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The larynx lies in the anterior part of the neck, in the midline, at the level of the third to sixth cervical vertebrae, and is held in position by muscles and ligaments. Above, the epiglottis is attached to the hyoid bone and the larynx opens into the lower part of the pharynx, so that the airway and the food passage share the same space for a few centimetres; below, the cricoid cartilage joins the first ring of the trachea. The thyroid gland wraps around its lower part and the upper trachea, and the great vessels of the neck run on either side. The whole organ rises and falls visibly during swallowing, and the laryngeal prominence of the thyroid cartilage (the 'Adam's apple') is usually more noticeable in men. The larynx is also smaller in women, which is one reason for the higher pitch of the female voice.

sections.heading: Cartilage skeleton
sections.body: The skeleton of the larynx consists of three unpaired midline cartilages and three pairs of smaller cartilages (arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform). From above downwards the main pieces are the epiglottis, thyroid cartilage, paired arytenoids with the small corniculates on their tips, and the cricoid. The thyroid cartilage is the largest, forming the front and sides of the voice box. The cricoid below it is the only complete cartilage ring in the larynx, shaped like a signet ring, wide at the back and narrow in front. The epiglottis is a flexible flap of elastic cartilage attached to the inside of the thyroid cartilage; during swallowing it folds back over the entrance to the airway. The arytenoids, perched on the back of the cricoid plate, are the most mobile part of the framework and carry the back ends of the vocal folds. The cricothyroid joints let the thyroid cartilage tilt on the cricoid, tightening the folds.

sections.heading: The glottis and vocal folds
sections.body: Inside, the larynx is divided into three regions: the supraglottis above the vocal folds, the glottis at their level, and the subglottis below, down to the lower edge of the cricoid. The glottis consists of the true vocal folds and the space between them (the rima glottidis); the vestibular folds belong to the supraglottis. The vestibular folds, or false vocal cords, are a pair of soft folds of mucous membrane lying above the true folds and help to close the airway during swallowing and straining. The true vocal folds are white, membranous folds attached by muscle to the thyroid cartilage in front and the arytenoid cartilages behind; each contains a vocal ligament, the free upper edge of the conus elasticus, with the vocalis muscle alongside it. Their pearly white colour, in contrast to the pink mucosa around them, makes them easy to identify when the larynx is viewed with an endoscope.

sections.heading: Muscles and nerves
sections.body: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx move the cartilages relative to one another and so control the position, length and tension of the vocal folds. The main ones are the cricothyroid, the thyroarytenoid, the lateral and posterior cricoarytenoid muscles and the interarytenoid (transverse and oblique arytenoid) muscles. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that opens (abducts) the folds for breathing; the others close them or adjust their tension for voice. Extrinsic muscles attached to the hyoid and sternum raise and lower the whole larynx during swallowing. Every intrinsic muscle except cricothyroid is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (a branch of the vagus), and cricothyroid by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which loops down into the chest before climbing back up beside the trachea to reach the larynx; this long course is why disease in the chest, including some lung cancers, can present as a hoarse voice.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The primary function of the larynx is to protect the lower respiratory tract from the aspiration of food into the trachea. During swallowing the larynx is pulled upwards and forwards, the epiglottis folds over the entrance, and the vestibular and vocal folds close tightly, so that the bolus passes around the closed airway into the oesophagus. A cough, which clears the airway if anything does get through, depends on the same closure: the folds shut, pressure builds in the chest, and they open suddenly to release a blast of air. For phonation the vocal folds are brought together and air driven up from the lungs sets them vibrating, producing sound that is shaped into speech by the pharynx, tongue, palate and lips; during quiet breathing the folds are held apart. Pitch is adjusted by lengthening and tensing the folds, and loudness by the force of the airflow.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance and investigation
sections.body: Laryngitis, in which the voice box or vocal folds become irritated or swollen, usually settles on its own within a week or two; symptoms that persist or keep recurring are checked by a GP. A hoarse voice that does not go away is the most common presenting feature of laryngeal cancer, and NHS guidance is that persistent unexplained hoarseness, especially with a lump in the neck, pain or difficulty swallowing, breathlessness, a persistent earache or unexplained weight loss, should prompt specialist referral. Reflux, vocal overuse, trauma and infection are other causes. The larynx is examined first by nasendoscopy, a thin flexible telescope passed through the nose, and, if the view is poor or an abnormality is seen, by laryngoscopy, in which a longer endoscope passed through the mouth gives a more detailed view and allows a biopsy. CT, MRI or PET-CT scans then show the extent of any cancer.

nose.title: Nose Anatomy
nose.descriptor: External Nose, Nasal Cavity, Septum & Conchae
nose.intro: The nose is the entrance to the respiratory tract and the organ of smell. The external nose, framed by the nasal bones above and flexible cartilages below, gives the face much of its character; inside, the nasal cavity is divided in two by the septum and its side walls carry the curled conchae, which warm, moisten and clean the air on its way to the lungs.

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: External nose and the internal nasal cavity

keyFacts.label: Skeleton
keyFacts.value: Paired nasal bones above; lateral and major alar cartilages and the septal cartilage below

keyFacts.label: Septum
keyFacts.value: A wall of bone (including the vomer) and cartilage separating the left and right nasal cavities

keyFacts.label: Conchae
keyFacts.value: Superior, middle and inferior conchae (turbinates) with the meatuses beneath them, increasing the surface area of the cavity

keyFacts.label: Nasal valve
keyFacts.value: The narrowest, flow-limiting segment, bordered by the upper lateral cartilage, the septum and the head of the inferior concha

keyFacts.label: Functions
keyFacts.value: Conducts, warms, humidifies and filters air; houses the sense of smell

keyFacts.label: Common problems
keyFacts.value: Nosebleeds, fractures, deviated septum, polyps, sinus and allergic disease

sections.heading: The external nose
sections.body: The external nose is the pyramid projecting from the middle of the face. It is convenient to think of it in thirds. The upper third is bony: the two nasal bones meet in the midline and articulate with the frontal bone above and the maxillae at the sides. The middle third is the cartilaginous vault, formed by the paired lateral (upper lateral) nasal cartilages that continue downwards from the nasal bones and by the upper edge of the septal cartilage between them. The lower third, the tip and nostrils, is shaped by the paired major alar cartilages, which curl around each nostril and give the tip its flexibility and spring. The nose is anatomically complex and varies widely between individuals, and because it plays a large part in facial appearance as well as in breathing, both aspects matter when an injury or an operation changes its shape.

sections.heading: The nasal cavity, septum and conchae
sections.body: Behind the nostrils the airway opens into the nasal cavity, a tall, narrow space extending back to the openings (choanae) into the nasopharynx. The septum, a wall of bone and cartilage, separates the left and right nasal cavities: its front part is the septal cartilage and its back and lower parts are bone, including the vomer. Each side wall carries three curled shelves of bone, the superior, middle and inferior nasal conchae (turbinates), covered in thick, vascular mucous membrane. Beneath each lies a passage, the superior, middle and inferior meatus, into which the sinuses and nasolacrimal duct drain; together the conchae and meatuses greatly expand the surface area of the cavity. Just inside each nostril the nasal valve, bordered by the upper lateral cartilage, the septum and the front of the inferior concha, is the narrowest part of the airway and limits airflow.

sections.heading: Lining, blood supply and nerves
sections.body: Most of the nasal cavity is lined by respiratory mucosa: a moist ciliated epithelium rich in mucus-secreting cells lying over a dense network of thin-walled blood vessels, especially on the conchae, where the blood flow can swell or shrink the lining to adjust the airway. The roof of the cavity and the upper septum carry the olfactory epithelium, which is essential to sensing odours; its receptor cells send fibres up through the roof of the nose to the olfactory bulbs of the brain. The lining is generously supplied with blood from branches of both the internal and external carotid systems, and these vessels run close to the surface, which is why the nose bleeds so readily and why most nosebleeds come from the soft front part of the septum. Sensation is carried by branches of the trigeminal nerve, so a blow to the nose is felt sharply and the nasal lining triggers sneezing when irritated.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The nose belongs to the conducting zone of the respiratory system: it moves air towards the lungs and conditions it on the way without itself taking part in gas exchange. The conchae and meatuses make the airstream swirl over a large area of warm, wet mucosa, which warms and humidifies incoming air so that it reaches the delicate lung tissue at body temperature and saturated with water vapour. At the same time the mucus traps dust, debris and pathogens, and the beating cilia sweep this mucus backwards to be swallowed, protecting the lower airway. The nasal valve regulates the rate of airflow and is the site of greatest resistance in the nasal airway. Finally, air drawn up to the roof of the cavity reaches the olfactory epithelium, giving the sense of smell and, with it, much of what is perceived as flavour.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance and investigation
sections.body: Because the nasal bones project from the face they are easily broken. Signs of a fracture include a crooked or misshapen nose, swelling and bruising, blocked nostrils and bleeding; most heal naturally without surgery; a nose that stays crooked or blocked can later be reset or the septum straightened. Clinicians look for a septal haematoma, a purple, boggy swelling of the septum that needs urgent drainage and antibiotics, and for clear fluid from one nostril, a possible cerebrospinal fluid leak. Nosebleeds are managed by sitting forward and pinching the soft part of the nose; persistent bleeding is cauterised or packed. Nasal polyps, fleshy swellings often linked to allergy or asthma, are treated first with steroid sprays or drops, with surgery for cases that do not respond; polyps can regrow. The cavity is examined with a speculum or endoscope, and CT shows the bones and sinuses.

oesophagus.title: Oesophagus Anatomy
oesophagus.descriptor: Course, Sphincters, Swallowing & the Gullet's Disorders
oesophagus.intro: The oesophagus, or gullet, is a muscular tube that carries swallowed food and drink from the pharynx in the neck, down through the chest behind the heart and great vessels, and through the diaphragm to the stomach. Rhythmic waves of muscle contraction push each mouthful along, and a sphincter at each end stops food and acid travelling the wrong way.

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Cervical, thoracic and abdominal portions

keyFacts.label: Start and finish
keyFacts.value: Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage in the neck and ends at the cardia of the stomach

keyFacts.label: Relations
keyFacts.value: Lies between the vertebral column and the trachea in the superior mediastinum, passing behind the arch of the aorta

keyFacts.label: Sphincters
keyFacts.value: Upper oesophageal sphincter of skeletal muscle; lower oesophageal sphincter of smooth muscle at the junction with the stomach

keyFacts.label: Lining
keyFacts.value: Pale pink flat (squamous) cells, which can change to red columnar cells in Barrett's oesophagus

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: Gastroscopy with biopsies; capsule-on-a-string (Cytosponge) test; barium swallow X-ray

sections.heading: Course and relations
sections.body: The oesophagus is divided into cervical, thoracic and abdominal parts. It begins in the neck at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, as a continuation of the pharynx, and lies behind the trachea and in front of the vertebral column. The thoracic part extends from the suprasternal notch to the diaphragm: in the superior mediastinum it still occupies the space between the vertebral column and the trachea, then it passes behind the arch of the aorta and the left main bronchus into the posterior mediastinum, where it lies behind the left atrium of the heart, separated only by the pericardium, before swinging forwards and to the left to reach the oesophageal hiatus. The short abdominal part runs from the hiatus to the cardia, where it joins the stomach.

sections.heading: Structure and sphincters
sections.body: The oesophagus has a mucosa, submucosa, muscular coat and outer connective tissue layer, with no serous covering in the chest. The mucosa is a tough, pale pink lining of flat squamous cells suited to the friction of swallowed food, and its glands secrete lubricating mucus. The muscular coat has inner circular and outer longitudinal layers; the upper third is mainly skeletal muscle, the middle third a mixture of skeletal and smooth muscle, and the lower third smooth muscle only. At the top, the upper oesophageal sphincter, a ring of skeletal muscle continuous with the lowest pharyngeal constrictor, regulates the movement of food from the pharynx into the oesophagus. At the bottom, the lower oesophageal sphincter, a thickening of smooth muscle reinforced by the right crus of the diaphragm, lets food pass into the stomach in one direction only.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: Each part of the oesophagus is supplied by nearby vessels: branches of the inferior thyroid arteries in the neck, oesophageal branches from the thoracic aorta and bronchial arteries in the chest, and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, which accompany it through the diaphragmatic hiatus, in the abdomen. Venous blood drains in the same segmental fashion, and at the lower end the veins draining to the left gastric vein connect with those draining upwards to the azygos system; when pressure in the liver circulation rises, as in cirrhosis, this connection distends into oesophageal varices that can bleed severely. The anterior and posterior vagal trunks (formed mainly from the left and right vagus nerves) lie on the lower oesophagus and pass with it through the hiatus; the vagus coordinates peristalsis and relaxes the lower sphincter, while sympathetic fibres run with the arteries.

sections.heading: Function: swallowing and peristalsis
sections.body: Swallowing, or deglutition, is a three-stage process. In the voluntary phase the tongue pushes the chewed bolus back from the mouth into the oropharynx. In the pharyngeal phase, a reflex, the soft palate rises to close off the nose, the larynx is pulled upwards, the epiglottis folds over the glottis to protect the airway, and the constrictor muscles of the pharynx contract in sequence, forcing the bolus through the relaxed upper sphincter into the oesophagus. This starts the oesophageal phase: rhythmic waves of peristalsis, beginning in the upper oesophagus, propel the bolus towards the stomach, so that food moves on even when a person is lying down. As the wave approaches, the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to admit the bolus and then closes again. The oesophagus digests nothing itself; its job is transport.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Weakness of the lower sphincter or a hiatus hernia lets stomach acid reflux into the oesophagus, producing heartburn. Long-standing reflux can change the lining of the lower oesophagus from flat, pale pink squamous cells to taller red columnar cells like those of the stomach, a condition called Barrett's oesophagus; it is more common in men and older people and carries a small yearly risk of turning into cancer, so people with Barrett's are offered surveillance gastroscopies with biopsies. Oesophageal cancer typically presents with food feeling stuck when eating, bringing food back up, or new indigestion or heartburn that persists for weeks; because these symptoms are easily confused with less serious conditions it is often found late, and NHS advice is that a persistent swallowing problem should never be ignored.

sections.heading: How the oesophagus is investigated
sections.body: The main test is gastroscopy (upper gastrointestinal endoscopy): an endoscopist passes a thin flexible tube with a camera in its tip through the mouth and down the oesophagus into the stomach, inspects the lining and, if necessary, takes small tissue samples (biopsies) for examination under a microscope. It also allows treatment such as stretching a narrowing. A less invasive screening test for Barrett's, the Cytosponge, uses a capsule on a string that is swallowed and then withdrawn, collecting cells from the lining as it passes; a positive result is usually followed by gastroscopy to confirm the diagnosis. A barium swallow is an X-ray examination taken while the patient swallows a contrast liquid, outlining the oesophagus and showing a narrowing, pouch or hernia. Manometry and acid monitoring assess the muscle, and CT and PET-CT stage cancer.

tongue.title: Tongue Anatomy
tongue.intro: The tongue is a muscular organ filling the floor of the mouth and extending back into the pharynx. Its muscles shape food into a bolus for swallowing and make it the most important articulator of speech, while its upper surface is studded with papillae that carry the taste buds and give it its rough texture.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Floor of the mouth, tethered beneath by the lingual frenulum; its base lies in the oropharynx

keyFacts.label: Muscles
keyFacts.value: Extrinsic muscles (including genioglossus and hyoglossus) move the tongue; intrinsic muscles change its shape

keyFacts.label: Papillae
keyFacts.value: Filiform, fungiform, foliate and circumvallate

keyFacts.label: Taste nerves
keyFacts.value: Chorda tympani (facial nerve) for the front of the tongue; glossopharyngeal nerve for the back

keyFacts.label: Glands
keyFacts.value: Lingual glands secrete mucus and a watery fluid containing lingual lipase

keyFacts.value: A mouth ulcer lasting more than three weeks, or a red or white patch or lump, should be checked by a GP or dentist

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The tongue occupies the oral cavity, resting against the hard and soft palate when the mouth is closed and surrounded by the lower teeth and gums. Its front two-thirds, the oral part, is free and mobile; the back third, the pharyngeal part or base, faces backwards into the oropharynx and lies in front of the epiglottis, with small pockets, the valleculae, between them where a swallowed pill or fish bone may lodge. On its under-surface a fold of mucous membrane, the lingual frenulum, tethers the tongue to the floor of the mouth; when this fold is unusually short or tight (tongue-tie) it can limit movement. The tongue is anchored below to the hyoid bone, in front to the mandible and above and behind to the styloid process of the skull and the soft palate, and these fixed points give its extrinsic muscles their leverage. The palatine tonsils lie at the sides of its base.

sections.heading: Muscles
sections.body: The tongue is almost entirely muscle, arranged in two groups. The extrinsic muscles arise from bone outside the tongue and move it as a whole: they pull it from side to side, poke it out and draw it back, which lets it manipulate food for chewing and shape it into a bolus. The genioglossus, a fan-shaped muscle running back from the inside of the chin, forms most of the tongue's bulk and pulls it forward, which is why lifting the jaw forward in an unconscious person keeps the tongue off the back of the throat. The hyoglossus, from the hyoid bone, retracts and depresses the tongue, aiding swallowing. The intrinsic muscles lie entirely within the tongue and run lengthwise, across and vertically; by shortening different sets the tongue can curl, flatten, narrow or point. This combination of coarse movement and fine shaping produces the rapid sequence of positions needed for speech.

sections.heading: Surface, papillae and taste buds
sections.body: The upper surface of the tongue is covered by four kinds of papillae. Filiform papillae are the most numerous; they carry touch receptors that help the tongue move food around, have no taste buds and give the tongue its rough surface. Fungiform papillae, scattered mainly over the front two-thirds, each hold a few taste buds and also sense pressure and temperature. Foliate papillae form folds along the sides towards the back, and the large circumvallate papillae, which contain the most taste buds, stand in a V-shaped row near the back margin. Taste buds occur in the fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae but never in the filiform ones, and their taste cells are replaced roughly every two weeks. Lingual glands beneath the surface secrete mucus and a watery fluid containing lingual lipase, an enzyme with a minor part in fat digestion that becomes active only in the stomach.

sections.heading: Nerves and blood supply
sections.body: Taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve that passes through the middle ear on its way to the brainstem; it can be damaged during middle ear surgery, operations on the mandible and tongue resections, leaving taste on the front of the tongue lost or altered. Taste from the back third travels in the glossopharyngeal nerve, and injury to it impairs taste there. General sensation from the front of the tongue is carried by a branch of the trigeminal nerve and from the back by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Nearly all the tongue's muscles are driven by the hypoglossal nerve, the twelfth cranial nerve, from the medulla; if it is damaged on one side the protruded tongue deviates towards the weak side. The tongue is richly vascular, supplied on each side by the lingual artery, so injuries bleed freely and heal quickly.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: The tongue forms early, at about the fourth week of development, when paired lateral lingual swellings and a midline swelling, the tuberculum impar, appear on the first pharyngeal arch. These enlarge and merge to form the front two-thirds of the tongue, while the back third develops from tissue of the later pharyngeal arches, which is why the two parts have different nerve supplies: trigeminal and facial for the front, glossopharyngeal for the back. The muscles migrate in from elsewhere, bringing the hypoglossal nerve with them. The line of union between the two parts persists as a V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, just behind the row of circumvallate papillae. Variations are common and usually harmless; the lingual frenulum may be short or attached far forward, producing tongue-tie, which is only treated if it interferes with feeding or speech.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: In babies, tongue-tie can make breastfeeding or bottle-feeding difficult; if it causes no problems treatment is not usually needed. Glossitis is a swollen, inflamed tongue that may become smooth, pale or bright red and sore; it is often a sign of another condition, and swelling that affects breathing is an emergency. The tongue is also a common site of mouth cancer. The NHS lists the warning symptoms as a mouth ulcer lasting more than three weeks, a red or white patch inside the mouth and a lump inside the mouth or on the lip; white patches on the tongue may be an early sign, and numbness or difficulty moving the tongue, chewing or swallowing can also occur. Early cancer can look like an ordinary ulcer, so any persistent change is examined by a GP or dentist and referred for specialist assessment; found early, a complete cure is possible in most cases.

trachea-bronchi.title: Trachea and Bronchial Tree Anatomy
trachea-bronchi.descriptor: Windpipe, Carina, Main Bronchi & Bronchopulmonary Segments
trachea-bronchi.intro: The trachea, or windpipe, is a rigid yet flexible tube that carries air from the larynx down through the neck and upper chest to the carina, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi. From there the airways branch again and again, like an upside-down tree, so that each lobe and each bronchopulmonary segment of the lungs receives its own bronchus.

keyFacts.label: Course
keyFacts.value: From the lower border of the larynx, down the midline of the neck and superior mediastinum, to the carina

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: C-shaped cartilage rings in front and at the sides, closed behind by a membrane containing smooth muscle

keyFacts.label: Carina
keyFacts.value: The cartilaginous keel at the bifurcation; highly sensitive, so touching it provokes coughing

keyFacts.label: Main bronchi
keyFacts.value: The right is wider and more vertical than the left, so inhaled objects more often lodge on the right

keyFacts.label: Lobar bronchi
keyFacts.value: Three on the right (upper, middle, lower) and two on the left

keyFacts.label: Segments
keyFacts.value: Each segmental bronchus supplies one bronchopulmonary segment: ten on the right, eight to ten on the left

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: Chest X-ray, CT and bronchoscopy, which can also remove inhaled objects

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The trachea begins where the cricoid cartilage of the larynx ends, in the lower neck, and descends in the midline in front of the oesophagus, which lies against its flat membranous back wall. In the neck it is covered by the isthmus of the thyroid gland and the strap muscles, and it is here that a tracheostomy opening is made when the upper airway is blocked. Passing behind the top of the breastbone it enters the superior mediastinum, where the arch of the aorta curves over the left main bronchus and the great veins and the thymus lie in front of it. It ends at the carina, the ridge at the point of division into the two main bronchi, which in an adult lies roughly at the level of the sternal angle. Each main bronchus runs outwards and downwards to the hilum of its lung, accompanied by the pulmonary artery and veins, nerves and lymph nodes.

sections.heading: Structure of the trachea and carina
sections.body: The tracheal wall is held open by a stack of C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, their open ends facing backwards; sources count between about fifteen and twenty of them. The gap at the back is bridged by a membrane containing smooth muscle (the trachealis) that can draw the ends of each ring together and narrow the airway, for example during coughing. Between the rings the wall is fibrous and elastic, allowing the trachea to lengthen as the larynx rises in swallowing and to bend with the neck. The inner lining is a ciliated mucous membrane that traps inhaled particles and sweeps them upwards. The carina is a cartilaginous projection from the lowest tracheal ring protruding into the lumen at the junction with the bronchi; through a bronchoscope it appears as a sharp keel-like ridge, and because it is very sensitive to touch, stimulating it evokes a vigorous cough.

sections.heading: Main, lobar and segmental bronchi
sections.body: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and steeper than the left, which is why an inhaled object most often ends up in the right lung. The right main bronchus divides into three lobar branches, for the upper, middle and lower lobes; the left gives two (the upper lobe bronchus also supplies the lingula). Each lobar bronchus then divides into segmental bronchi, each supplying one bronchopulmonary segment, the largest subdivision of a lobe. There are ten segments in the right lung and eight to ten in the left; the right upper lobe, for example, has apical, posterior and anterior segments and the middle lobe lateral and medial ones. Unlike the tracheal rings, the bronchial wall is supported by irregular plates of cartilage, which make it more deformable; down the tree the cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases, until the bronchioles have none.

sections.heading: Blood supply and nerves
sections.body: The airways themselves are nourished not by the pulmonary circulation but by small bronchial arteries: the left arise directly from the thoracic aorta and the single right bronchial artery usually from the third or fourth posterior intercostal artery; they run along the bronchi into the lungs and supply their walls down to the bronchioles. Venous blood returns partly through bronchial veins to the azygos system and partly into the pulmonary veins. The trachea and bronchi are richly innervated by branches of the vagus nerve and sympathetic trunk through the pulmonary plexuses: vagal fibres constrict the smooth muscle and increase mucus secretion, sympathetic fibres relax it, and sensory vagal endings in the lining, densest at the carina and the branch points, trigger the cough reflex when touched or irritated. This is the nervous pathway that inhaled drugs for asthma exploit and that makes a bronchoscope so provocative without local anaesthetic.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The trachea and bronchi belong to the conducting zone of the respiratory system: they move air to and from the gas-exchanging tissue of the lungs but do not exchange gases themselves. The cartilage keeps the airway open against the negative pressure of inspiration, while the smooth muscle and the branching pattern let the system adjust resistance and distribute air between segments. The ciliated lining, mucus and cough reflex together form the lungs' main defence against inhaled dust, microbes and food, carrying debris up to the larynx to be swallowed or coughed out. The membranous back wall of the trachea allows the oesophagus behind it to expand as a bolus of food passes.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance and investigation
sections.body: A blockage in the trachea threatens life immediately, whereas one in a bronchus collapses only the lung beyond it. Inhaled foreign bodies are a particular hazard in young children. NHS guidance is that a child with a significant choking or inhalation history should be referred urgently to the ear, nose and throat team even if they seem well, because the examination may be entirely normal early on and this does not exclude a foreign body; the child is usually admitted for observation and probable bronchoscopy, which both confirms the diagnosis and removes the object. A total blockage of the airway requires emergency help. The airways are examined with chest X-ray, CT, which displays the whole tree, and bronchoscopy, in which a flexible or rigid telescope inspects the carina and bronchi, takes samples and retrieves objects. Post-intubation narrowing, tumours and asthma are other disorders.

skull.title: Skull Anatomy
skull.descriptor: Bones of the Skull, Sutures, Foramina & Head Injuries
skull.intro: The skull is formed by 22 bones in two groups, the brain case and the face. The brain case surrounds and protects the brain, while the facial bones give the face its structure and form the upper and lower jaws. Only the mandible, or lower jaw, is movable; the other bones are immobile and united into a single unit by fibrous joints called sutures. The 3D model shows each bone separately and also includes the hyoid bone, which is not part of the skull.

sections.heading: Brain case and facial bones
sections.body: The skull has two regions: the neurocranium, or brain case, which protects the brain, and the viscerocranium, which forms the face. The brain case is made up of eight bones: the paired parietal and temporal bones and the single frontal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones. The face has fourteen bones: the paired maxilla, palatine, zygomatic, nasal and lacrimal bones and inferior nasal conchae, and the single vomer and mandible. The ethmoid is counted among the cranial bones but also contributes to the formation of facial structures. The hyoid bone is an independent bone that does not contact any other bone and so is not part of the skull.

sections.heading: Sutures
sections.body: Sutures are fibrous joints in which connective tissue binds adjacent skull bones together. The coronal suture runs from side to side across the skull and joins the frontal bone to the right and left parietal bones. The sagittal suture extends backwards from the coronal suture, running along the midline at the top of the skull, and joins the two parietal bones. The lambdoid suture joins the occipital bone to the right and left parietal and temporal bones. The squamous suture unites the squamous part of the temporal bone with the parietal bone. Skull sutures are functionally classed as synarthroses, which are essentially immobile joints, although some allow slight movement.

sections.heading: Mandible and jaw joint
sections.body: The mandible, or lower jaw, is the only movable bone of the skull. The mandible has a horizontal body and a vertical ramus on each side, and the outer margin where they join is the angle. The coronoid process on the ramus gives attachment to one of the biting muscles, while the condylar process is topped by the oval condyle. The condyle meets the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone at the temporomandibular joint, where an articular disc lies between the bones. The joint allows the mandible to be lowered and raised, which opens and closes the mouth, to move forwards and backwards, and to move from side to side. The masseter, the main muscle used for chewing, arises from the zygomatic arch and raises the mandible to close the mouth.

sections.heading: Cranial floor and openings
sections.body: The floor of the cranial cavity forms three fossae that become deeper from front to back. The anterior fossa is the shallowest and extends from the frontal bone to the lesser wings of the sphenoid. The middle fossa lies behind it, and its floor holds the optic canal, superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum. The posterior fossa is the deepest, extending to the occipital bone, and contains the foramen magnum, internal acoustic meatus, jugular foramina and hypoglossal canals. The skull base has many openings through which nerves and blood vessels pass. The foramen magnum is the largest of the cranial foramina, and its contents include the brainstem and the vertebral arteries. The optic canal transmits the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery.

sections.heading: Orbits, nose and sinuses
sections.body: Seven bones contribute to the walls of each orbit, or eye socket, which houses the eyeball and the muscles that move it: the frontal, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, ethmoid, lacrimal and sphenoid bones. The nasal septum divides the nasal cavity into halves and is formed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone, which makes up its upper portion, together with the vomer and septal cartilage. The paranasal sinuses sit within the frontal, maxillary, sphenoid and ethmoid bones: the frontal sinus is the most anterior, the maxillary sinuses, below the orbits, are the largest, and the sphenoid sinus is the most posterior. The ethmoid bone contains the ethmoid air cells, small air spaces between the orbit and the upper nasal cavity.

sections.heading: Growth and changes with age
sections.body: At birth, large areas of dense connective tissue called fontanelles lie between the bones of the brain case. The fontanelles provide flexibility to the skull during birth, allowing it to change shape as it passes through the birth canal. After birth the fontanelles allow for continued growth of the skull, and they decrease in size and eventually disappear. The flat bones of the brain case form by intramembranous ossification, in which mesenchyme cells differentiate directly into bone-producing cells, whereas the floor of the brain case forms by endochondral ossification, in which a cartilage model is gradually converted into bone. Late in life the sagittal, coronal and lambdoid sutures begin to ossify and fuse, a change called synostosis, or bony fusion.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: At the pterion, where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet just above the ear, a blow to the side of the skull can tear the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, and cause an epidural haematoma. Arterial bleeding into the epidural space accumulates quickly and does not cross suture lines. Temporomandibular joint disorder can arise from arthritis, wearing of the articular cartilage, muscle fatigue from overuse or grinding of the teeth, damage to the articular disc or a jaw injury. The NHS lists pain around the jaw, ear and temple, and clicking, popping or grinding sounds when the jaw moves, among the symptoms of temporomandibular disorder.

sections.heading: Head injuries and skull fractures
sections.body: Most head injuries are not serious, but the NHS says it is important to get medical help for any symptoms. The NHS lists a head wound with something inside it, a dent to the head and clear fluid coming from the ears or nose among the signs for which it advises calling 999. For a severe head injury, a CT scan produces a detailed image of the inside of the head that shows whether there is any bleeding, bruising or swelling in the brain. Skull X-rays are not carried out any more because they do not provide information on brain damage. Most skull fractures heal by themselves, particularly simple linear fractures, although healing can take many months.

hand.title: Hand Bones Anatomy
hand.descriptor: Carpals, Metacarpals, Phalanges, Carpal Tunnel & Fractures
hand.intro: Each hand consists of 27 bones: eight carpal bones in the wrist, five metacarpal bones forming the palm and fourteen phalanges in the thumb and fingers. The carpal bones lie in two rows of four, and only the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum contribute to the radiocarpal (wrist) joint. The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, often as a result of a fall onto the hand.

sections.heading: Bones of the hand
sections.body: The eight carpal bones make up the wrist, the five metacarpal bones form the palm and the fourteen phalanges form the thumb and fingers. The metacarpals are numbered one to five starting from the thumb side. The first metacarpal is freely mobile, moving independently of the others, which join together to make up the palm. The thumb has only two phalanges, a proximal and a distal, while each of the other four digits, from the index finger to the little finger, has a proximal, middle and distal phalanx. The expanded distal end of each metacarpal articulates with the proximal phalanx of the thumb or one of the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joint, and also forms the knuckles of the hand.

sections.heading: Carpal bones
sections.body: The eight carpal bones are arranged in two rows of four, a proximal row and a distal row. Counting from the thumb side, the proximal row is the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform, and the distal row is the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate. Several names describe shape: scaphoid means boat-shaped, lunate moon-shaped, triquetrum three-cornered, pisiform pea-shaped, capitate head-shaped and hamate hooked. The pisiform can be felt as a bony bump at the medial base of the hand, and the hamate has a prominent bony extension on its anterior side, the hook of the hamate. Only the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum contribute to the radiocarpal joint: the scaphoid and lunate articulate directly with the distal end of the radius, whereas the triquetrum articulates with a fibrocartilaginous pad.

sections.heading: The carpal tunnel
sections.body: The flexor retinaculum is a fibrous connective tissue band that forms the anterior roof of the carpal tunnel at the wrist, and many experts consider it synonymous with the transverse carpal ligament. Posterior to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel, lie the four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, the four flexor digitorum profundus tendons, the flexor pollicis longus tendon and the median nerve. Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve at the wrist, causing hand pain, numbness and tingling in the area the nerve supplies. As the condition advances there can be weakness and eventual wasting of the thenar muscles at the base of the thumb. Raised pressure within the carpal tunnel is the primary factor in the onset of the condition, although in most cases the underlying cause is unknown.

sections.heading: Fractures of the wrist and scaphoid
sections.body: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, and NHS trust leaflets describe it as a small bone of the hand on the thumb side of the wrist. Scaphoid fractures and wrist fractures usually result from a fall onto an outstretched hand. A scaphoid injury typically causes pain and tenderness near the base of the thumb, and the wrist may swell, but most scaphoid fractures leave the wrist looking normal and cause only mild symptoms. Some people also have difficulty gripping or twisting the wrist or thumb. One NHS trust page on distal radial fractures, which are breaks of the forearm bone next to the wrist joint, describes immediate severe pain, swelling and often deformity of the wrist, painful movement, and sometimes tingling or numbness in the fingers. Wrist fractures are common in young children and older people.

sections.heading: How scaphoid injuries are investigated
sections.body: A scaphoid fracture does not always show on the first X-ray, and in some people it is not obvious until some days after the injury. If the first X-ray does not show a fracture but one is still suspected, the person is examined again and the X-ray repeated at the fracture clinic, and an MRI scan is requested if suspicion continues. One NHS trust leaflet explains that, until a fracture can be ruled out, the wrist is treated as if the bone were broken, because the scaphoid has a poor blood supply. An X-ray is a quick, painless procedure that produces images of the inside of the body. The person needs to keep still during the exposure so the picture is not blurred, and more than one X-ray may be taken from different angles.

adrenals.title: Adrenal Glands Anatomy
adrenals.intro: The adrenal glands are a pair of small, triangular endocrine glands, one lying on the upper surface of each kidney. Each has an outer cortex that makes steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone, and an inner medulla that makes adrenaline and noradrenaline for the fight-or-flight response. Together they help the body respond to stress and regulate salt and water balance.

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body:
Each adrenal gland is a small, triangular organ that sits on the upper surface of a kidney, within the renal (Gerota's) fascia. The glands are also known as the suprarenal glands. The two glands differ in shape: the right gland is pyramidal, whereas the left is crescentic (crescent-shaped). The right gland lies below the liver, behind the inferior vena cava and in front of the diaphragm.

The two layers of each gland have different embryonic origins: the cortex is derived from mesoderm, whereas the medulla is derived from neural crest cells.

sections.heading: Cortex and medulla
sections.body: Each gland has an outer cortex of glandular tissue and an inner medulla of nervous tissue, all surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. The cortex is organised into three zones, and each zone makes a different class of steroid hormone from cholesterol. The outermost zona glomerulosa makes mineralocorticoids, mainly aldosterone, which affect body minerals, especially sodium and potassium. The middle zona fasciculata makes glucocorticoids, chiefly cortisol, which raise blood glucose levels. The innermost zona reticularis makes androgens, a class of steroid sex hormones. The medulla at the core of the gland makes the amine hormones adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine), and adrenaline is made in greater quantities.

sections.heading: Blood supply and nerves
sections.body: The adrenal glands are among the most well-perfused organs in the body. Arterial blood reaches each gland from several sources: the superior suprarenal arteries (branches of the inferior phrenic arteries), the middle suprarenal arteries (from the abdominal aorta) and the inferior suprarenal arteries (from the renal arteries). Each gland is often drained by a single adrenal vein, although variations are common, particularly on the left. The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right adrenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The medulla receives preganglionic sympathetic nerve fibres, which release acetylcholine to stimulate the release of adrenaline and noradrenaline.

sections.heading: Hormones and their control
sections.body:
The medulla drives the short-term fight-or-flight response: adrenaline, together with noradrenaline, prepares the body for action and is released in response to sympathetic nervous system signals. The cortex drives the long-term response, through a pathway that runs from the hypothalamus, through ACTH released from the anterior pituitary, to the release of cortisol from the cortex.

Cortisol regulates a wide range of processes, including metabolism and the immune response, and has an important role in helping the body respond to stress. Cortisol has a negative feedback loop that acts on the hypothalamus, anterior pituitary and adrenal gland to inhibit the release of corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH), ACTH and cortisol. Aldosterone's main role is to regulate salt and water in the body, which affects blood pressure. The renin-angiotensin system also drives aldosterone release, because angiotensin II stimulates the zona glomerulosa to make aldosterone.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: underactive adrenal glands
sections.body: Adrenal problems can arise when the glands are overactive or underactive. In Addison's disease, also called primary adrenal insufficiency, the glands are underactive and the cortex fails to supply cortisol, aldosterone and sex steroids. In developed countries, autoimmune disease is the usual cause: the immune system targets the outer layer of the adrenal gland, which disrupts production of cortisol and aldosterone. Early symptoms can resemble depression or flu. Common symptoms include fatigue, muscle weakness, loss of appetite and weight loss, and people with Addison's disease may also have darkening of the skin. An adrenal crisis is the most serious complication of adrenal insufficiency and is a medical emergency.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: excess hormones and tumours
sections.body:
Cushing's syndrome is caused by too much cortisol in the body. Long-term use of high-dose steroid medicine is the most common cause, and tumours of the pituitary or adrenal glands, usually non-cancerous, can also cause it; when the pituitary is responsible it is called Cushing's disease. Features include more body fat on the neck, upper back, chest and tummy, a red, round face, easy bruising, stretch marks and muscle weakness.

In primary hyperaldosteronism, the adrenal glands make too much aldosterone, and blood pressure can become very high. A non-cancerous tumour in one adrenal gland, called an aldosterone-producing adenoma, is a common cause. Cancer can also arise in the gland: for adrenocortical carcinoma, surgery to remove the adrenal gland (adrenalectomy) is often used. Phaeochromocytoma is a rare tumour of adrenal gland tissue that releases too much adrenaline and noradrenaline, and most people with it have attacks of symptoms such as headaches, palpitations, sweating and high blood pressure.

sections.heading: How the adrenal glands are investigated
sections.body: Because the symptoms of Addison's disease come on slowly, they may be overlooked or confused with other illnesses. In suspected Addison's disease, blood tests measure the levels of sodium, potassium and cortisol. The ACTH stimulation test is the test used most often to diagnose adrenal insufficiency, and blood tests can also detect antibodies in autoimmune Addison's disease. For suspected Cushing's syndrome, cortisol can be checked in blood, urine or saliva, and a high result may lead to referral to an endocrinologist (a hormone specialist), who may arrange further tests on the pituitary and adrenal glands, such as blood tests and scans. For Cushing's syndrome, diagnosis is based on the medical history, a physical examination and laboratory tests.

small-intestine.title: Small Intestine Anatomy
small-intestine.descriptor: Duodenum, Jejunum, Ileum, Villi & Blood Supply
small-intestine.intro: The small intestine is the part of the digestive tract that runs from the pylorus of the stomach to the ileocaecal valve, where it meets the large intestine. It has three regions, the duodenum, jejunum and ileum, and it is the site of most chemical digestion and almost all absorption. Intestinal brush border enzymes and pancreatic enzymes do most of the chemical digestion, and bile salts emulsify lipids, which increases the surface area available to lipases.

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The three regions follow one another from the stomach, with no clear dividing line between the jejunum and the ileum. The duodenum lies below the stomach, and its C-shaped curve surrounds the head of the pancreas. Its first part is intraperitoneal, whereas its second, third and fourth parts are retroperitoneal, lying behind the peritoneum. The jejunum and ileum are also intraperitoneal, and the mesentery carries their blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen and the ileum mainly in the right lower quadrant. The ileum ends at the ileocaecal valve, where the small intestine meets the large intestine.

sections.heading: Regions
sections.body: The duodenum is the shortest part of the small intestine, and it has four parts: the bulb, the descending part, the horizontal part and the ascending part. Bile and pancreatic juice enter the second (descending) part of the duodenum through the hepatopancreatic ampulla, also called the ampulla of Vater, which forms where the common bile duct meets the pancreatic duct. The ileum, the final region, is the longest part of the small intestine. In life the whole small intestine is about three metres long, and in a cadaver it is about twice as long. The regions also differ in what they absorb: the duodenum and upper jejunum are the main sites of iron absorption, while the terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12, which needs intrinsic factor made in the stomach.

sections.heading: Wall and lining
sections.body: The wall of the small intestine has four layers: the mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria and serosa. Circular folds (plicae circulares), villi and microvilli together greatly increase the surface area available for absorption. The microvilli give the mucosa a fuzzy appearance called the brush border, and enzymes that finish the digestion of carbohydrates and proteins are fixed to the membranes of the microvilli. The cells of the epithelium and intestinal glands include absorptive cells, goblet cells (which secrete mucus), Paneth cells (which secrete lysozyme) and enteroendocrine cells (which release hormones). Intestinal juice is a mixture of water and mucus. The epithelial cells are renewed rapidly.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: The small intestine receives arterial blood from the coeliac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery. The proximal duodenum is supplied mainly from the coeliac trunk through the gastroduodenal artery, and the distal duodenum from the superior mesenteric artery; the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, which arise from these two sources, anastomose. The jejunum and ileum are supplied by jejunal and ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery, which run through the mesentery. Veins follow the arterial supply and drain into the superior mesenteric vein, which joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. Lymph begins in the mucosa and drains to nodes along the mesentery, the arterial arcades and the superior mesenteric artery, and from there to the coeliac nodes. The lesser splanchnic presynaptic sympathetic fibres synapse in the superior mesenteric ganglia, and sympathetic fibres decrease small intestinal secretions and motility and cause vasoconstriction.

sections.heading: Function: digestion and absorption
sections.body:
Bile salts emulsify lipids, and the pancreas supplies lipid-digesting enzymes such as lipase. Pancreatic amylase and brush-border disaccharidases such as maltase and sucrase digest carbohydrates, and the pancreas secretes protein-digesting enzymes such as trypsin and chymotrypsin. Brush-border enzymes then complete the digestion of carbohydrates and proteins.

Blood capillaries in the villi take up sugars and amino acids, while the lacteals take up fat. Inside the intestinal cells, fats are reassembled into triglycerides and packaged with other lipids and proteins into chylomicrons, which are too big to pass through the basement membranes of blood capillaries and so enter the large pores of the lacteals. Water absorption is thought to occur through osmotic gradients and aquaporins in the intestinal membranes. Segmentation separates chyme and then pushes it back together, mixing it and providing time for digestion and absorption.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body:
Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition in which gluten causes damage to the lining of the small bowel: the finger-like villi flatten, which reduces the surface area available for absorption and can lead to nutrient deficiencies. Crohn's disease is a long-term condition in which abnormal immune reactions cause inflammation in the digestive tract, most commonly in the small intestine and the beginning of the large intestine. Ulcers can form in the stomach or in the duodenum, and the NHS says stomach ulcers are usually caused by H. pylori infection or by taking anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs).

Short bowel syndrome develops when the small intestine is shortened or damaged and cannot absorb enough nutrients, most often after surgery to remove part of it. Small intestine cancers include adenocarcinoma, sarcoma, carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumours, gastrointestinal stromal tumours and lymphoma; unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain can be signs, although other conditions can cause the same signs and symptoms. Persistent symptoms should be assessed by a clinician.

sections.heading: How the small intestine is investigated
sections.body: A gastroscopy checks inside the food pipe, the stomach and the top of the intestine using a thin tube with a camera, and a small sample of cells (a biopsy) may be collected. The top of the intestine is the duodenum, the first region of the small intestine. The NHS says a gastroscopy can also be used for treatment, for example to stop bleeding inside the stomach or food pipe or to remove growths. For coeliac disease, the NHS describes two main methods of diagnosis: a blood test for coeliac antibodies and a biopsy of the small intestine taken with an endoscope passed through the mouth.

bladder.title: Bladder Anatomy
bladder.descriptor: Wall, Trigone, Urethra, Blood Supply & Control
bladder.intro: The urinary bladder is a hollow, muscular organ in the pelvis that collects urine from the ureters. To empty it, the brain signals the sphincters to relax and then signals the muscular bladder wall to tighten, squeezing urine through the urethra. While the bladder fills, the sphincter muscles stay contracted to keep urine in. The urethra arises from the base of the bladder and carries urine out of the body.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Lesser pelvis just behind the pubic symphysis in adults; extends into the abdominal cavity when full

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: Urothelial lining, lamina propria, detrusor smooth muscle and an outer serosa or adventitia

keyFacts.label: Trigone
keyFacts.value: Triangular area of the bladder floor with corners at the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening; the most sensitive region for stretch receptors

keyFacts.label: Sphincters
keyFacts.value: Involuntary internal sphincter of smooth muscle and voluntary external sphincter of skeletal muscle

keyFacts.label: Arteries
keyFacts.value: Superior and inferior vesical arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries

keyFacts.label: Lymph drainage
keyFacts.value: Mostly to the external iliac nodes

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: Cystoscopy, a thin camera tube passed through the urethra into the bladder

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: In adults the bladder lies in the lesser pelvis when it is empty, just behind the pubic symphysis, and extends into the abdominal cavity when it is full. It is described as having four parts: the apex or dome, the body, the fundus, and the neck. Peritoneum covers the superior surface and part of the posterior surface of the bladder. Where a prostate is present, the rectum lies behind the bladder and the prostate lies immediately below it. Where a vagina is present, its anterior wall lies behind the bladder. The muscles of the pelvic diaphragm support the bladder from below.

sections.heading: Wall, lining and trigone
sections.body: The bladder wall is made up of an inner urothelial lining, the lamina propria beneath it, the detrusor muscle (the muscularis propria) and an outer serosa or adventitia. The urothelium has more layers when the bladder is relaxed and reorganises into fewer layers as the bladder fills, without structural damage. The detrusor is made of crisscrossing bands of smooth muscle, and the whole organ is highly stretchable. On the inner surface the trigone is a triangular area of the bladder floor whose corners are the two ureteric openings and the opening of the urethra. It is the most sensitive region of the bladder for stretch receptors.

sections.heading: Urethra and sphincters
sections.body: The urethra begins at the trigone area at the base of the bladder. The male urethra passes through the prostate gland just below the bladder and also carries semen. There are two urethral sphincters, an internal one and an external one, which differ in tissue type and control. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle at the bladder neck, continuous with the detrusor, and works involuntarily; in the male urethra it also helps stop semen flowing back into the bladder during ejaculation. The external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control and is supplied by the pudendal nerve. Urinary incontinence is commonly linked to problems with the urethral sphincters.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: The superior and inferior vesical arteries provide the blood supply to the bladder, with the superior vesical artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery, supplying the upper part. Where a vagina is present, the vaginal artery replaces the inferior vesical artery. Venous blood drains through the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac vein, and lymph drains mostly to the external iliac nodes. The bladder receives parasympathetic, sympathetic and somatic nerve fibres, and the parasympathetic fibres arise from the sacral spinal nerves and form the pelvic splanchnic nerves. Sympathetic activity, through the hypogastric nerves, suppresses contraction of the detrusor, whereas parasympathetic activity contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter. Sensory information from the upper bladder wall follows the sympathetic pathway, whereas that from the lower part follows the parasympathetic nerves.

sections.heading: Storage and voiding
sections.body: The bladder acts as a reservoir for urine. Urination alternates between a storage phase, when urine collects, and a voiding phase, when the bladder empties. During storage the detrusor, the muscle of the bladder wall, stays relaxed as the bladder fills, while the sphincter muscles stay contracted to keep urine in. Sympathetic tone to the bladder, carried by the hypogastric nerves, keeps the detrusor relaxed, and somatic stimulation through the pudendal nerve keeps the external sphincter closed. Voiding begins with increased sensory input from the detrusor, and higher brain centres start voluntary voiding. In the brainstem, the pontine micturition centre, also known as Barrington's nucleus, is the hub of the voiding reflex. The detrusor then contracts, the sphincters relax and urine flows out through the urethra.

sections.heading: Infection and bladder pain
sections.body: Cystitis is a bladder infection. It often gets better by itself, but may sometimes be treated with antibiotics. Symptoms include pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often and urgently, dark, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and pain low in the tummy. The shorter female urethra contributes to the higher incidence of bladder infections in females. The NHS says pain in the back, a high temperature or feeling sick can point to a kidney infection, which needs prompt treatment. The NHS advises seeing a GP for cystitis symptoms in children and in people with a prostate. Interstitial cystitis, also called bladder pain syndrome, is a chronic, or long-lasting, condition in which there is pain in the bladder. The pain tends to intensify as urine accumulates and to ease once the bladder is emptied, and severity varies from mild pelvic pressure or tenderness to intense bladder pain.

sections.heading: Incontinence and bladder cancer
sections.body: The NHS describes several types of urinary incontinence. In stress incontinence urine leaks out at times when the bladder is under pressure, for example when coughing or laughing. Urge incontinence is a sudden and very intense need to pass urine that cannot be delayed, and it is usually linked to overactivity of the detrusor muscle, known as an overactive bladder. Almost all bladder cancers are urothelial carcinomas, which start in the urothelial cells that line the bladder and other urinary organs. Blood in the urine is the most common symptom of bladder cancer; it may look pink, red or dark brown, may come and go, or may be found only on a laboratory test. It can also have other causes, such as urinary tract infections or kidney or bladder stones, but the NHS advises having blood in the urine checked by a GP even when there are no other symptoms.

sections.heading: How the bladder is investigated
sections.body: Cystoscopy lets a clinician look inside the bladder. A thin tube with a camera is gently passed into the urethra and moved through it into the bladder. In a flexible cystoscopy, local anaesthetic gel numbs the urethra and saline is run into the bladder to inflate it, which makes it easier to see inside. At cystoscopy the examiner inspects the bladder floor and trigone and records the number and position of the ureteric openings. For suspected bladder cancer the NCI says a doctor may order urine tests first and that cystoscopy is the most useful diagnostic test.
