pelvic-girdle.title: Pelvis Anatomy
pelvic-girdle.descriptor: Hip Bones, Sacrum, Pelvic Brim, Joints & Fractures
pelvic-girdle.intro: The bony pelvis is made up of the two hip bones together with the sacrum and the coccyx. It links the spine and the lower limbs, and it carries the weight of the trunk down to the legs during standing and walking. The pelvic cavity inside the bony ring houses the urinary bladder, rectum and internal reproductive organs, which the pelvis helps to protect.

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx

keyFacts.label: Each hip bone
keyFacts.value: Formed from the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse during the late teenage years

keyFacts.label: Joints
keyFacts.value: Pubic symphysis at the front, sacroiliac joints at the back and the sacrococcygeal joint between sacrum and coccyx

keyFacts.label: Divisions
keyFacts.value: False (greater) pelvis above the pelvic brim and true (lesser) pelvis below it

keyFacts.label: Landmarks
keyFacts.value: Iliac crest, ischial spine, ischial tuberosity, obturator foramen and acetabulum

keyFacts.label: Function
keyFacts.value: Supports the upper body, passes its weight to the lower limbs and helps to protect the pelvic organs

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: CT helps to assess the pelvis and detect bleeding after injury

sections.heading: The hip bone
sections.body: The hip bone, also called the coxal bone, is one of two bones that together with the sacrum and coccyx make up the pelvis. Each adult hip bone is formed by three separate bones, the ilium, ischium and pubis, that fuse together during the late teenage years. The ilium is the upper, fan-shaped and largest part, and its curved upper margin is the iliac crest. The ischium forms the posteroinferior part and bears the ischial tuberosity, a large roughened area that carries the weight of the body when sitting. The pubis forms the anterior part and curves medially to join the pubis of the opposite hip bone at the pubic symphysis. The three bones converge to form the acetabulum, a deep, cup-shaped cavity on the lateral side of each hip bone that is part of the hip joint.

sections.heading: Landmarks and muscle attachments
sections.body: The iliac crest ends at the rounded anterior superior iliac spine in front and the posterior superior iliac spine behind, and the anterior inferior and posterior inferior iliac spines lie below them. On the posterior margin of the ilium the greater sciatic notch, a large U-shaped indentation, lies above the ischial spine, the bony projection that separates it from the lesser sciatic notch. The obturator foramen is the large opening at the front of the hip bone, between the ischium and pubis. The ischial tuberosity also serves as the attachment for the posterior thigh muscles.

sections.heading: Sacrum, coccyx, joints and ligaments
sections.body: The midline sacrum and coccyx complete the bony pelvis. At the front the two hip bones meet at the pubic symphysis, and at the back each hip bone unites with the sacrum at a sacroiliac joint. The coccyx attaches to the sacrum at the sacrococcygeal joint. The anterior, posterior and interosseous sacroiliac ligaments each contribute to stabilising the sacroiliac joint, and the interosseous ligament forms the main connection between the sacrum and ilium. The sacroiliac joint is supplied by several arteries, including the iliolumbar, superior gluteal and lateral sacral arteries. The sacrotuberous ligament runs from the sacrum to the ischial tuberosity, and the sacrospinous ligament is a triangular band from the ischial spine to the sacrum and coccyx. Together these two ligaments form the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, and the pudendal nerve lies between them.

sections.heading: The true and false pelvis
sections.body: The pelvic brim, also called the pelvic inlet, separates the true pelvis from the false pelvis above it. It begins at the sacral promontory behind and the pubic symphysis in front, and its boundary landmarks also include the pectineal and arcuate lines. The broad false (greater) pelvis lies above the brim, is formed by the wings of the ilium and belongs to the abdomen. The narrower true (lesser) pelvis lies below the brim and is bounded below by the pelvic outlet, which is bounded by the coccyx, the ischial tuberosities and the pubic symphysis. The true pelvis holds the urinary bladder, rectum and part of the colon, and also the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries in people who have them.

sections.heading: Shape differences between pelvises
sections.body: OpenStax describes general differences between the female and male pelvis, and says the female pelvis is wider to accommodate childbirth. It describes the female pelvis as having a larger subpubic angle, a rounder pelvic brim and a wider, shallower lesser pelvic cavity. The female sacrum is described as wider, shorter and less curved, with a sacral promontory that projects less into the pelvic cavity, which gives the inlet a rounder or oval outline. The greater sciatic notch is described as broader in the female pelvis, and in general the bones of the male pelvis are thicker and heavier.

sections.heading: Function and blood supply
sections.body: The main role of the pelvic girdle is to support the upper body and transfer body weight to the lower limbs. StatPearls describes the hip bone as forming a sturdy basin that supports the trunk and provides attachment for lower limb muscles and ligaments. In females, the pelvic outlet also offers support and guidance for a foetus through the birth canal. The internal iliac artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions: the anterior supplies the pelvic organs, the perineum and the gluteal and adductor areas, and the posterior supplies the parietal structures of the pelvis and the gluteal region.

sections.heading: Pelvic and hip fractures
sections.body:
A fracture of the pubic rami, which are parts of the pubis at the front of the pelvis, most often follows a fall from standing. Falls are common in older people, and people are more prone to these fractures if their bones are thin (osteoporosis). A Frimley Health NHS leaflet says that pain usually increases with movement and weight bearing, and NHS trust leaflets say that these fractures are usually managed without surgery. In injuries that disrupt the pelvic ring, the posterior pelvic venous plexus is the main source of haemorrhage.

A hip fracture is a different injury, a break in the top of the thigh bone close to the hip joint, usually caused by a fall or an injury to the side of the hip.

sections.heading: Pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy
sections.body: Healthier Together, an NHS Wales site, describes pelvic girdle pain in pregnancy as a collection of uncomfortable symptoms caused by stiffness of the pelvic joints, or the joints moving unevenly, at the back or front of the pelvis. Pain can be felt over the pubic bone at the front and across one or both sides of the lower back, and it can spread into the thighs. The NHS advises speaking to a midwife or GP if pelvic pain makes it hard to move around.

sections.heading: How the pelvis is investigated
sections.body: A hip fracture is usually first suspected from the symptoms, a physical examination and the history of the injury, and imaging such as an X-ray, an MRI scan or a CT scan is used to confirm it. For pelvic injuries, StatPearls notes that CT helps to assess the pelvis and detect bleeding, and cautions clinicians not to assume that a pelvic ring injury is the only source of bleeding, with chest and abdominal bleeding excluded first. An X-ray examination usually takes only a few minutes and nothing is felt during the exposure; the person needs to keep still so that the image is not blurred, and several X-rays may be taken from different angles.

testes.title: Testicle Anatomy
testes.descriptor: Scrotum, Epididymis, Sperm Production, Torsion & Cancer
testes.intro: The testes, also called the testicles, are a pair of egg-shaped glands that lie in the scrotum, the sac of loose skin below the penis. They make sperm and the hormone testosterone. Sperm pass from each testis into the epididymis, a coiled tube in which they mature, and then along the deferent duct, which joins the duct of the seminal vesicle near the prostate to form the ejaculatory duct. The seminal vesicles lie behind the prostate and add fluid to the semen.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: A pair of egg-shaped glands inside the scrotum

keyFacts.label: Coverings
keyFacts.value: Outer tunica vaginalis, then the tough tunica albuginea, which folds inwards to divide the testis into lobules

keyFacts.label: Working tissue
keyFacts.value: Seminiferous tubules make sperm; Leydig cells between the tubules make testosterone

keyFacts.label: Sperm pathway
keyFacts.value: Epididymis (head, body and tail), then the deferent duct, which joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct

keyFacts.label: Temperature
keyFacts.value: Kept a few degrees below core body temperature, helped by the dartos and cremaster muscles

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Testicular arteries from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries; veins form the pampiniform plexus

keyFacts.label: Investigation
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound scan of the testicles and blood tests when testicular cancer is suspected

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: Each testis lies in its own compartment of the scrotum, separated from the other testis by the scrotal septum. The dartos muscle forms the muscle layer beneath the scrotal skin and continues inwards to form that septum. Each testis is covered on the outside by the tunica vaginalis, and beneath this lies the tough, white tunica albuginea. The deferent duct is bundled with blood vessels and nerves in the spermatic cord, which supports the testis in the scrotum.

sections.heading: Structure of the testis
sections.body:
The tunica albuginea folds inwards to form septa that divide the testis into hundreds of lobules, and at the back of the testis it folds in to form the mediastinum testis, an incomplete septum. The tightly coiled seminiferous tubules form the bulk of each testis, and sperm are made within them. The seminiferous tubules join straight tubules, the tubuli recti, which lead to the rete testis, a network in the mediastinum testis, and efferent ductules then connect the rete testis to the epididymis.

Leydig cells, which lie between the tubules, make testosterone. Sertoli cells help control the survival of the developing germ cells, and tight junctions between them form the blood-testis barrier. This barrier keeps bloodborne substances away from the germ cells and stops surface antigens on developing germ cells from escaping into the bloodstream and provoking an autoimmune response.

sections.heading: Epididymis, deferent duct and seminal vesicle
sections.body:
The epididymis is a coiled tube with a head, a body and a tail. Sperm continue to mature as they pass through it and are stored in the tail until ejaculation. The deferent duct is also known as the vas deferens or ductus deferens. It continues from the tail of the epididymis, and during ejaculation contraction of smooth muscle pushes sperm from the tail into the duct.

The deferent duct ascends through the inguinal canal into the pelvic cavity, looping behind and to the side of the prostate. Its ampulla joins the duct of the seminal vesicle at the base of the prostate to form the ejaculatory duct, which enters the prostate and empties into the prostatic urethra. Each seminal vesicle lies in the pelvis behind the prostate, below the fundus of the bladder and above the rectum, beside the ampulla of the deferent duct.

sections.heading: Blood supply, nerves and lymph
sections.body: The testicular arteries arise from the front and side of the abdominal aorta, just below the origin of the renal arteries, with additional supply from the artery of the vas deferens and the cremasteric artery. Venous blood leaves through the pampiniform plexus, a network of veins that lies in front of the deferent duct. The testes receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibres. Lymph from the testes travels with the testicular vessels and drains to the para-aortic lymph nodes, which lie beside the aorta. The arteries to the seminal vesicles come from the middle and inferior vesical arteries and the middle rectal artery.

sections.heading: Function: sperm, testosterone and temperature
sections.body:
The testes make sperm and the androgen testosterone, and luteinising hormone binds to receptors on the Leydig cells and increases their production of testosterone.

Sperm production proceeds more efficiently when the testes are kept a few degrees below core body temperature. In cold weather the dartos and cremaster muscles contract to lift the testes towards the body and reduce the surface area of the scrotum, which retains heat; when the temperature rises the scrotum relaxes, which increases its surface area and promotes heat loss.

During ejaculation sperm travel through the deferent duct and mix with fluid from the associated seminal vesicle.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: torsion and infection
sections.body: In testicular torsion the spermatic cord twists, which cuts off the blood supply to the testicle and can cause lasting damage. Sudden, severe pain in one testicle is the most common sign, and NHS advice is to go straight to A&E or call 999. Epididymitis is swelling and pain of the epididymis, the tube behind the testicle, and the NHS says it is usually caused by a sexually transmitted infection or a urine infection, with other causes including mumps, tuberculosis and a groin injury. Depending on the cause, there may also be difficulty passing urine or a discharge from the penis.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: swellings and undescended testes
sections.body:
Most testicular lumps and swellings are not cancer, although the NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in a testicle. Cystic swellings are usually caused by a hydrocele, a cyst in the epididymis or a varicocele, and these are all benign and need treatment only if they cause significant symptoms. A hydrocele is fluid that collects between the layers of the tunica vaginalis, and a varicocele is an abnormal widening of the veins of the pampiniform plexus that usually occurs on the left.

An undescended testicle has not moved into the scrotum as it usually does, and the condition is common in young boys. Often the testicle moves into place on its own, but sometimes surgery is needed, and the problem is usually found at the newborn examination. Left untreated, an undescended testicle can lead to fertility problems later in life and an increased risk of testicular cancer, and it can also twist (testicular torsion), which can be painful.

sections.heading: Testicular cancer and how it is investigated
sections.body: Testicular cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissue of one or both testicles. The NHS lists a lump or swelling in a testicle, a testicle getting bigger, an ache or pain in the testicle or scrotum, and a heavy, firm or hard scrotum as the main symptoms. Having these symptoms does not definitely mean testicular cancer, but the NHS advises seeing a GP about any of them. A scrotal ultrasound scan will usually distinguish between benign and cancerous swellings. When testicular cancer is suspected, the NHS lists blood tests and an ultrasound scan of the testicles among the tests used, after which a specialist explains the results and the next steps.

foot.title: Foot Anatomy
foot.intro: The skeleton of the foot is built from twenty-six bones: seven tarsals forming the heel and midfoot, five metatarsals forming the forefoot, and fourteen phalanges in the toes. Arranged as a set of arches and bound by strong plantar ligaments, these bones carry the whole weight of the body on a small base, absorb the shock of each step and act as a rigid lever when the calf muscles push the body forwards.

keyFacts.label: Bones
keyFacts.value: 26 per foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals and 14 phalanges (two in the big toe, three in each of the others)

keyFacts.label: Tarsals
keyFacts.value: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms

keyFacts.label: Largest bone
keyFacts.value: Calcaneus, which forms the heel and receives the Achilles tendon

keyFacts.label: Ankle joint
keyFacts.value: Talus articulating with the distal tibia, the medial malleolus of the tibia and the lateral malleolus of the fibula

keyFacts.label: Arches
keyFacts.value: Medial and lateral longitudinal arches (tarsals behind, metatarsals in front) and a transverse arch; flattening is pes planus (flat foot)

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries, whose branches anastomose around the joints

keyFacts.label: Nerves
keyFacts.value: Medial and lateral plantar nerves to the sole, deep fibular nerve to the dorsum of the tarsal joints, plantar digital nerves to the toe joints

sections.heading: Location and regions
sections.body: The foot lies at right angles to the leg below the ankle, and its skeleton is described in three regions. The hindfoot is the talus and calcaneus; the midfoot is the navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms; and the forefoot is the five metatarsals and the phalanges of the toes. The talus is the keystone: it sits in the mortise formed by the tibia and fibula at the ankle, rests on the calcaneus below and projects its rounded head forwards into the navicular, so that all the weight from the leg passes through it before being shared between the heel behind and the ball of the foot in front. No muscle attaches to the talus, and most of its surface is covered by articular cartilage. The weight-bearing points on the ground are the heel, the heads of the metatarsals and, at the side, the lateral border of the foot; the medial border is normally raised off the ground by the arch.

sections.heading: Bones
sections.body: OpenStax describes the seven tarsals forming the posterior half of the foot, with the talus most superior and the calcaneus, the largest bone of the foot, beneath it forming the heel. In front of the talus the boat-shaped navicular lies medially; in front of the calcaneus the cuboid lies laterally; and the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms sit in a row between the navicular and the first three metatarsals. The five metatarsals, numbered from the medial side, each have a base, shaft and head: the first is short and thick because it bears the most load, the second is the longest and is locked between the cuneiforms, and the fifth has a tuberosity on its base that is felt on the outer edge of the foot. The big toe has two phalanges and each other toe three, and two sesamoid bones under the head of the first metatarsal take the weight at push-off.

sections.heading: Joints, ligaments and arches
sections.body: The talocrural (ankle) joint is a hinge for dorsiflexion and plantarflexion. Beneath it the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints allow inversion and eversion, tilting the sole to adapt to uneven ground; the tarsometatarsal and intertarsal joints allow only slight gliding, and the metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints flex and extend the toes. StatPearls lists the calcaneofibular, talocalcaneal, calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular ligaments stabilising the calcaneus, with the plantar aponeurosis and long plantar ligament supporting the arch. OpenStax describes the longitudinal arches as tarsals behind and metatarsals in front, united by strong ligaments that resist collapse under weight; the spring ligament under the head of the talus supports the medial arch, and the plantar fascia, running from the calcaneus in five bands to the toes, acts as a tie-beam.

sections.heading: Blood supply and nerves
sections.body: According to StatPearls, the foot is supplied mainly by the dorsalis pedis artery on the dorsum and the posterior tibial artery, which passes behind the medial malleolus and divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries; their branches anastomose around the joints, each joint fed by whichever reaches it. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are the standard checks of circulation to the foot. The plantar side of the tarsal joints is innervated by the medial and lateral plantar nerves, branches of the tibial nerve, and the dorsal side by the deep fibular nerve; the metatarsophalangeal joints depend mainly on plantar digital nerves, and the interphalangeal joints receive the medial dorsal cutaneous branch of the superficial fibular nerve and the plantar interdigital nerves. The plantar fascia is supplied by the plantar nerves and small branches of the posterior tibial artery.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The foot has two conflicting jobs: to be supple enough to mould itself to the ground and absorb impact, and stiff enough to act as a lever. It achieves both through its arches. At heel strike the arches flatten slightly and the ligaments and plantar fascia stretch, storing energy and spreading the load across the heel and metatarsal heads; as the body moves forwards and the toes extend, the plantar fascia tightens like a windlass, the arch rises and the tarsal joints lock, converting the foot into a rigid beam through which the calf muscles, pulling on the calcaneus, lift the body onto the ball of the foot. The subtalar and transverse tarsal joints let the heel and forefoot twist relative to each other so that the sole stays flat on sloping surfaces, and the short muscles of the sole fine-tune the arches with every step. The big toe provides the final push and helps with balance.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Fractures of the toes and metatarsals follow stubbing, crushing, twisting falls and repetitive loading (stress fractures). NHS leaflets describe pain, swelling and tenderness over the fracture, bruising, difficulty walking or taking weight and, in the toes, bleeding or discolouration under the nail. Only an X-ray can confirm a fracture, but a lesser toe in normal alignment is usually treated without one, whereas the big toe, a deformed toe or tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal is X-rayed to confirm and classify the injury. Reduced mobility afterwards carries a risk of a blood clot, so calf pain or breathlessness needs urgent assessment. Other disorders include pes planus, plantar fasciitis at the calcaneal attachment of the fascia, hallux valgus, calcaneal fractures and Lisfranc injuries of the tarsometatarsal joints, often missed on plain films and needing CT.

gallbladder.title: Gallbladder Anatomy
gallbladder.descriptor: Bile Ducts, Cystic Duct, Blood Supply & Bile Flow
gallbladder.intro: The gallbladder is a pear-shaped sac tucked under the right lobe of the liver that stores and concentrates bile between meals. Bile made by liver cells drains through the hepatic ducts into the common hepatic duct, which joins the cystic duct from the gallbladder to form the common bile duct; this carries bile to the duodenum, where it meets the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Fossa on the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver, in the right upper quadrant

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Fundus, body, infundibulum (Hartmann's pouch) and neck leading to the cystic duct

keyFacts.label: Duct system
keyFacts.value: Right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, cystic duct, common bile duct

keyFacts.label: Calot's triangle
keyFacts.value: Bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior margin of the liver; contains the cystic artery

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Cystic artery, usually a branch of the right hepatic artery

keyFacts.label: Function
keyFacts.value: Stores bile and concentrates it by reabsorbing water and ions, up to about tenfold

keyFacts.label: Control
keyFacts.value: Cholecystokinin from the duodenum triggers gallbladder contraction and bile release

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The gallbladder lies in a shallow fossa on the under-surface of the right lobe of the liver, with its rounded fundus projecting just beyond the liver's inferior margin so that it touches the anterior abdominal wall near the tip of the ninth right costal cartilage. Its body is in contact with the first part of the duodenum and the transverse colon, and its neck points towards the porta hepatis, where the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein enter and leave the liver. The extrahepatic bile ducts run within the free edge of the lesser omentum, with the common bile duct lying to the right of the hepatic artery and in front of the portal vein, before the duct passes behind the first part of the duodenum and the head of the pancreas to reach the second part of the duodenum.

sections.heading: Parts and duct system
sections.body: The gallbladder has a fundus, a body and a neck. The body narrows through an asymmetric infundibulum, Hartmann's pouch, into the neck, which in most people connects to the common bile duct through a single cystic duct. Bile produced by hepatocytes passes along ductules into bile ducts that merge into the right and left hepatic ducts, then into the common hepatic duct. After leaving the gallbladder the cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct, which carries bile towards the small intestine. Near the duodenum the common bile duct meets the pancreatic duct at a shared opening, the hepatopancreatic ampulla, guarded by a sphincter of smooth muscle. The cystic duct usually joins the extrahepatic bile duct about halfway between the porta hepatis and the ampulla, most often on its medial side, although the level and side of the junction vary.

sections.heading: Blood supply, innervation and Calot's triangle
sections.body: The cystic artery, usually a branch of the right hepatic artery, supplies the gallbladder and cystic duct, and it lies within Calot's triangle, the space bounded by the cystic duct laterally, the common hepatic duct medially and the inferior margin of the liver above. The cystic lymph node (the node of Lund, or Calot's node) also lies within the triangle. Venous blood from the gallbladder drains partly through small veins directly into the liver and partly through a cystic vein to the portal system. Autonomic nerves reach the gallbladder with the vessels: parasympathetic fibres from the vagus and sympathetic fibres from the coeliac plexus, with sensory fibres that explain why gallbladder pain is felt in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant and, when the diaphragm is irritated, referred to the right shoulder.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The gallbladder's two main jobs are to store bile and to concentrate it. Between meals the sphincter at the ampulla is closed, so bile backs up the common bile duct and cystic duct into the gallbladder, whose lining reabsorbs water and ions until the bile is up to about ten times more concentrated than when it left the liver. When fatty chyme enters the duodenum, the duodenal hormone cholecystokinin triggers contraction of the gallbladder wall and relaxation of the sphincter, releasing bile alongside pancreatic enzyme secretion. Bile salts and phospholipids then break large fat globules into small droplets, a step needed for lipid digestion and absorption. Most bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum and return to the liver to be secreted again.

sections.heading: Variation
sections.body: The biliary tree is one of the most variable regions of abdominal anatomy, which matters because it is operated on so often. The cystic duct may be long or short, may run parallel to the common hepatic duct for some distance before joining it, or may enter on the right, left or posterior aspect. The cystic artery may arise from the common or left hepatic artery, may be double, or may cross in front of the common hepatic duct. Accessory hepatic ducts and a right hepatic duct draining into the cystic duct are recognised traps. Identifying Calot's triangle and dissecting it until only two structures, the cystic duct and cystic artery, are seen entering the gallbladder is the basis of the 'critical view of safety' that surgeons use to avoid injuring the bile ducts or hepatic artery during cholecystectomy.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Gallstones form when concentrated bile precipitates cholesterol or pigment, and most cause no symptoms. A stone obstructing the cystic duct causes biliary colic, severe pain in the upper abdomen often on the right side, and if the obstruction persists, inflammation of the gallbladder. A stone that passes into the common bile duct blocks bile flow, causing jaundice and infection, and because the duct shares its opening with the pancreatic duct it can also provoke pancreatitis. Diagnosis rests on the symptoms, right upper abdominal tenderness, blood tests and ultrasound, with MR cholangiopancreatography when duct stones are suspected. The main treatment is cholecystectomy, removal of the gallbladder, while duct stones can be cleared by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography. During surgery the common bile duct can be mistaken for the cystic duct and is at risk of transection.

penis.title: Penis Anatomy
penis.descriptor: Erectile Bodies, Glans, Urethra, Blood Supply, Innervation & Erection
penis.intro: The penis is the male organ of copulation and the final conduit for urine. It is built around three cylinders of erectile tissue: two corpora cavernosa, which form the bulk of the shaft, and the corpus spongiosum, which surrounds the spongy urethra and expands at the tip into the glans. Erection is a vascular event, driven by nitric oxide released from nerve endings that relaxes the smooth muscle of the penile arteries so that blood fills the erectile tissue faster than it can leave.

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Root (bulb and crura, fixed in the perineum), body or shaft, and glans

keyFacts.label: Erectile bodies
keyFacts.value: Paired corpora cavernosa dorsally; single corpus spongiosum ventrally around the urethra

keyFacts.label: Glans
keyFacts.value: Expansion of the corpus spongiosum, densely supplied with nerve endings, covered by the prepuce (foreskin)

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Branches of the internal pudendal artery: deep (cavernous), dorsal and bulbar arteries

keyFacts.label: Venous drainage
keyFacts.value: Deep dorsal vein to the prostatic plexus; superficial dorsal vein to the external pudendal veins

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Dorsal nerve of the penis (pudendal nerve) for sensation; cavernous nerves from the prostatic plexus for erection

keyFacts.label: Function
keyFacts.value: Erection, ejaculation of semen and passage of urine through the spongy urethra

sections.heading: Location and parts
sections.body: The penis is divided into a root, a body and a glans. The root lies hidden in the superficial perineal space below the pelvic floor: the bulb of the penis is attached to the perineal membrane in the midline and is pierced by the urethra, while the two crura are anchored to the ischiopubic rami on either side. These three masses converge in front of the pubic symphysis to form the body, or shaft, which hangs free and is suspended from the pubis by the suspensory and fundiform ligaments. The body ends in the glans, whose expanded rim, the corona, overhangs a shallow groove, the neck. In the uncircumcised penis a double fold of skin, the prepuce or foreskin, forms a collar around the glans that protects and lubricates it. The skin of the shaft is thin, hairless and loosely attached, allowing it to move during erection.

sections.heading: Erectile bodies and urethra
sections.body: Each of the two larger, lateral chambers is a corpus cavernosum, and together they make up the bulk of the penis. They lie side by side on the dorsal aspect of the shaft, enclosed in a dense fibrous tunica albuginea, and are connected through fenestrations in the septum between them so that blood moves freely from one to the other. Below them lies the corpus spongiosum, a smaller chamber that surrounds the spongy, or penile, urethra and can be felt as a raised ridge on the erect penis; proximally it expands into the bulb and distally into the glans. The tunica albuginea of the corpus spongiosum is thinner and more elastic than that of the corpora cavernosa, so the spongiosum stays less rigid during erection and the urethra within it can distend to allow semen to pass. The urethra opens at the external urethral meatus on the tip of the glans.

sections.heading: Blood supply and venous drainage
sections.body: Branches of the internal pudendal arteries are the main suppliers of blood to the penis. The deep arteries of the penis run in the centre of each corpus cavernosum and give off helicine arteries that open into the cavernous spaces to supply the erectile tissue. The arteries of the bulb supply the bulbous part of the corpus spongiosum, the urethra and the bulbourethral gland. The dorsal arteries run along the dorsal vein between the corpora cavernosa to supply the fibrous tissue around the corpora, the corpus spongiosum, the spongy urethra and the penile skin. Venous blood from the erectile tissue collects in the deep dorsal vein, which passes beneath the pubic symphysis to the prostatic venous plexus, while the skin drains through the superficial dorsal vein to the external pudendal veins. Lymph drains to the superficial and deep inguinal and the internal iliac nodes.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sensation from the skin of the penis and the glans travels in the dorsal nerve of the penis, a terminal branch of the pudendal nerve. The glans has a high concentration of nerve endings, giving very sensitive skin that influences the likelihood of ejaculation. The erectile tissue is controlled by autonomic fibres. Parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves pass through the prostatic plexus and continue as the cavernous nerves, which run beside the prostate and under the pubic symphysis to the corpora cavernosa, prostate and urethra; these fibres release nitric oxide and are pro-erectile. Sympathetic fibres from the hypogastric nerves bring about ejaculation and return the penis to the flaccid state. The pudendal nerve also supplies the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles, which compress the root of the penis.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: During sexual arousal, nitric oxide is released from nerve endings near the blood vessels within the corpora cavernosa and spongiosum. It induces relaxation of the smooth muscle surrounding the penile arteries, producing the vasodilation necessary for erection: the helicine arteries open and blood floods the cavernous spaces, which expand against the tunica albuginea and compress the small veins that drain them. The result of increased blood flow into the penis and reduced blood return from it is erection; the stiff tunica of the corpora cavernosa converts the raised pressure into rigidity, while the more elastic spongiosum keeps the urethra open for ejaculation. At ejaculation, sympathetic activity contracts the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate, and the perineal muscles propel semen along the urethra, which when flaccid carries urine.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Because erection depends on intact arteries, nerves and hormones, diseases affecting any of these can cause erectile dysfunction; diabetes, certain medicines and psychological factors also contribute, and prostate or bladder cancer surgery can injure the nearby cavernous nerves and arteries. Assessment includes a genital examination looking for hypogonadism, phimosis, penile lesions or a palpable plaque. In Peyronie's disease a fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea causes curvature or deformity of the erect penis, often with pain and some erectile dysfunction; its cause is unknown and may be autoimmune. Phimosis, a foreskin too tight to retract over the glans, and Peyronie's disease are anatomical findings that prompt referral to andrology. Priapism, a prolonged erection, is treated by aspirating blood from the corpora, possible because the two corpora communicate.

pituitary.title: Pituitary Gland Anatomy
pituitary.descriptor: Hormones, Lobes, Blood Supply & Hypothalamic Connection
pituitary.intro: The pituitary is a pea-sized gland that hangs from the base of the brain on a thin stalk and sits in a bony cup, the sella turcica, in the sphenoid bone. It has two lobes with different origins and different ways of working: the anterior lobe makes and releases hormones under orders carried from the hypothalamus in a private portal blood system, while the posterior lobe stores and releases hormones made in the hypothalamus itself. Its output controls growth, the thyroid and adrenal glands, the gonads, lactation and water balance.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, below the hypothalamus and optic chiasm, between the cavernous sinuses

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Anterior lobe (adenohypophysis), posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) and a thin pars intermedia between them

keyFacts.label: Connection to the brain
keyFacts.value: Pituitary stalk (infundibulum) carrying the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal veins and the axons of hypothalamic neurons

keyFacts.label: Anterior lobe hormones
keyFacts.value: Growth hormone, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH and prolactin

keyFacts.label: Posterior lobe hormones
keyFacts.value: Anti-diuretic hormone (vasopressin) and oxytocin, made in the hypothalamus

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Superior hypophyseal arteries feed the portal system of the anterior lobe; inferior hypophyseal arteries feed the posterior lobe; short veins drain to the dural venous sinuses

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI is the imaging method of choice for pituitary disease

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The pituitary occupies the sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression in the body of the sphenoid bone at the centre of the skull base. A fold of dura, the diaphragma sellae, roofs the fossa and is pierced by the pituitary stalk, which rises to the hypothalamus. Immediately above the diaphragm lies the optic chiasm, so a gland that enlarges upwards presses first on the crossing fibres from the nasal halves of both retinas and classically narrows the outer halves of both visual fields. On each side of the fossa is a cavernous sinus containing the internal carotid artery and the nerves to the eye muscles. Below, only a thin plate of bone separates the gland from the sphenoid air sinus, which is the route used in transsphenoidal pituitary surgery, approached through the nose.

sections.heading: Lobes and origin
sections.body: The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) is glandular tissue that develops from an upgrowth of the roof of the embryonic mouth (Rathke's pouch), whereas the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) is nervous tissue that grows down from the floor of the developing brain and keeps its connection as the infundibulum or stalk. Between them lies a narrow pars intermedia, whose cells produce melanocyte-stimulating hormone among other products. The anterior lobe is the larger and contains several populations of hormone-secreting cells; the posterior lobe contains no secretory cell bodies at all, only the axon endings of hypothalamic neurons and their supporting cells. Remnants of Rathke's pouch may persist as small cysts in the adult gland.

sections.heading: Blood supply and the portal system
sections.body: The gland is supplied by hypophyseal branches of the internal carotid arteries. The paired superior hypophyseal arteries form a primary capillary plexus in the median eminence at the top of the stalk, where hypothalamic neurons release their regulating hormones. This blood is collected into hypophyseal portal veins that run down the stalk and open into a second plexus of fenestrated capillaries among the cells of the anterior lobe, so hypothalamic signals reach the anterior pituitary undiluted and in high concentration. Small superior hypophyseal branches also reach the stalk, optic nerves and chiasm, the intermediate lobe is fed by anastomoses between the anterior and posterior capillary beds, and the posterior lobe receives the inferior hypophyseal arteries directly. Short veins drain the gland into the neighbouring dural venous sinuses and so into the systemic circulation.

sections.heading: Hormones and control
sections.body: The anterior pituitary produces six main hormones in response to releasing or inhibitory signals from the hypothalamus and to feedback from the level of circulating hormones: adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), which acts on the adrenal cortex to drive cortisol release; growth hormone, stimulated by growth hormone-releasing hormone and inhibited by somatostatin; thyroid-stimulating hormone; the two gonadotrophins, luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone; and prolactin. The posterior pituitary does not make hormones. Anti-diuretic hormone (vasopressin), which controls water balance and blood pressure, and oxytocin, which drives uterine contractions in labour and milk release during breastfeeding, are synthesised in the hypothalamus, carried down the axons of the stalk and stored in the posterior lobe until nerve impulses release them into the blood.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The pituitary is the link between the nervous system and the endocrine system. Hypothalamic neurons sense the body's state, including blood osmolality, stress, temperature, light and the levels of thyroid, adrenal and sex hormones, and translate it into pulses of releasing hormones that set the pituitary's output. Each pituitary hormone then controls a distant target: growth hormone acts on bone, muscle and the liver; TSH on the thyroid; ACTH on the adrenal cortex; LH and FSH on the ovaries and testes; prolactin on the breast; ADH on the kidney's collecting ducts; and oxytocin on the uterus and breast. Negative feedback from the target glands' hormones on both the hypothalamus and pituitary keeps each axis stable, which is why measuring a pituitary hormone together with its target hormone tells a clinician where in the axis a fault lies.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Most pituitary disease is caused by benign adenomas. The National Cancer Institute's PDQ summary notes that symptoms depend on whether a tumour over-produces a hormone, under-produces hormones by compressing the normal gland, or presses on neighbouring structures, causing headache, blurred or double vision, loss of the outer visual fields and drooping eyelids. Hypopituitarism, described by the Society for Endocrinology, is under-production of one or more pituitary hormones after tumours, surgery, radiotherapy, injury or inflammation. Investigation pairs each pituitary hormone with its target hormone, tests the visual fields and images the gland: MRI is the modality of choice for its soft-tissue contrast, with CT less sensitive. Sudden headache with visual loss and collapse suggests pituitary apoplexy, bleeding into or infarction of a tumour, an emergency.

prostate.title: Prostate Anatomy
prostate.descriptor: Zones, Lobes, Blood Supply, Innervation & Function
prostate.intro: The prostate is a walnut-shaped gland that sits at the base of the bladder and surrounds the first part of the urethra. It receives sperm and seminal vesicle fluid through the ejaculatory ducts and adds its own thin, milky, alkaline secretion to form semen. Its position against the front wall of the rectum allows it to be examined by digital rectal examination, and its growth in later life can obstruct the urethra that runs through it.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Below the neck of the bladder, in front of the rectum and behind the pubic symphysis, resting on the pelvic floor

keyFacts.label: Lobes
keyFacts.value: Clinically a right lateral, left lateral and median lobe; anatomically described as five lobes

keyFacts.label: Zones
keyFacts.value: Peripheral, central and transition zones with an anterior fibromuscular stroma; the central zone forms the base and surrounds the ejaculatory ducts

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Mainly the inferior vesical artery, with contributions from the middle rectal and internal pudendal arteries

keyFacts.label: Venous drainage
keyFacts.value: Prostatic venous plexus to the internal iliac veins

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Autonomic fibres from the inferior hypogastric plexus: sympathetic via the hypogastric nerve, parasympathetic via the pelvic splanchnic nerves

keyFacts.label: Secretion
keyFacts.value: Thin, milky fluid containing citrate, enzymes and prostate-specific antigen

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The prostate lies in the lesser pelvis immediately below the neck of the bladder, with its base fused to the bladder and its apex resting on the external urethral sphincter and the pelvic floor. The prostatic urethra passes through it from base to apex, so the gland is often described as doughnut-shaped. In front, a fat-filled retropubic space separates it from the pubic symphysis; behind, only the thin rectovesical fascia separates its posterior surface from the anterior wall of the rectum, which is why the gland can be palpated through the rectum and sampled by transrectal biopsy. On each side the levator ani muscles cradle it, and the seminal vesicles and ampullae of the vasa deferentia lie against its upper posterior surface before their ejaculatory ducts enter the gland.

sections.heading: Lobes and zones
sections.body: Anatomically the prostate has traditionally been split into five lobes, but in clinical practice it is described as having two lateral lobes, right and left, separated by a shallow posterior groove, and a median lobe lying between the urethra and the ejaculatory ducts. Histologically a three-zone model is more useful. The central zone forms the base of the gland and encircles the ejaculatory ducts as they run down to open on either side of the seminal colliculus in the prostatic urethra. The peripheral zone makes up most of the glandular tissue, lies posteriorly and laterally, and is the part felt on rectal examination. The transition zone surrounds the urethra above the ejaculatory ducts and is the zone that enlarges with age. In front of the urethra the gland is largely non-glandular anterior fibromuscular stroma, continuous with the smooth muscle of the bladder neck.

sections.heading: Blood supply, lymphatics and innervation
sections.body: The inferior vesical artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery, is the main supplier of the prostate, with the middle rectal and internal pudendal arteries contributing as well. Venous blood drains through the prostatic venous plexus, between the gland and its fibrous sheath, into the internal iliac veins; the plexus also communicates with the vertebral venous plexuses, a route by which prostate cancer can spread to the spine. Lymphatics drain to the internal iliac and sacral nodes. Autonomic fibres reach the gland from the inferior hypogastric plexus: sympathetic input via the hypogastric nerve drives contraction of the glandular smooth muscle at ejaculation, while parasympathetic supply comes from the pelvic splanchnic nerves through the prostatic plexus, whose cavernous branches continue forwards to the penis. Sensory fibres travel in the hypogastric and pelvic plexuses.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The prostate is an accessory gland of the reproductive system. During ejaculation it receives sperm and seminal vesicle fluid from the ejaculatory ducts and adds its own alkaline secretion to the mixture as it passes through the prostatic urethra; the seminal vesicles and prostate together contribute most of the volume of semen, with sperm making up only a small share. The glandular tissue makes a thin, milky fluid that contains citrate, which acts as a nutrient for sperm, enzymes, and prostate-specific antigen. The prostatic enzymes help the semen first to clot and then to liquefy after ejaculation, which allows the sperm to move onwards in the female reproductive tract. The smooth muscle of the gland and bladder neck contracts at the same time, expelling the secretion and closing the bladder neck so that semen is directed forwards rather than into the bladder.

sections.heading: Development and age change
sections.body: The prostate develops in fetal life as buds of epithelium growing out from the urethra into the surrounding mesenchyme, a process driven by androgens made by the fetal testes; the central zone is thought to have a different embryological origin, related to the Wolffian ducts, from the rest of the gland, which may explain why it rarely gives rise to disease. The gland remains small until puberty, when testosterone causes it to grow to its adult size. From middle age onwards the transition zone around the urethra tends to enlarge again as benign nodules form, slowly compressing the prostatic urethra, whereas the peripheral zone is the usual site of cancer. Because these two processes affect different zones, a gland can be enlarged without harbouring cancer and can harbour cancer without being enlarged.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Benign enlargement compresses the urethra and causes weak urine flow, hesitancy and incomplete emptying; advanced prostate cancer can produce the same symptoms, while early prostate cancer may cause no symptoms at all. Assessment begins with a digital rectal examination of the posterior surface of the gland and a blood test for prostate-specific antigen. A raised PSA has benign causes, including enlargement and prostatitis, and rectal examination alone is poor at detecting cancer, so multiparametric MRI is increasingly used before biopsy to target suspicious areas and avoid unnecessary sampling; only a biopsy, usually guided by transrectal ultrasound or MRI fusion, confirms the diagnosis. Obstruction is relieved by transurethral resection, and the closeness of the cavernous nerves to the capsule explains the risk of erectile dysfunction after radical prostatectomy.

rib-cage.title: Rib Cage Anatomy
rib-cage.descriptor: Sternum, Ribs, Costal Cartilages, Joints & Breathing Movements
rib-cage.intro: The rib cage, or thoracic cage, is the bony and cartilaginous frame of the chest: the sternum in front, twelve pairs of ribs curving round from the thoracic vertebrae behind, and the costal cartilages that join most of the ribs to the sternum. It shields the heart, lungs and great vessels, gives attachment to the muscles of breathing and of the upper limb, and, because its joints allow the ribs to swing up and out, it changes the volume of the chest with every breath.

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The thoracic cage encloses the thoracic cavity and extends from the thoracic inlet, bounded by the first ribs and the top of the manubrium, down to the diaphragm, which attaches around its lower margin. In front it is the sternum, flat and palpable along its whole length; behind, the ribs articulate with the twelve thoracic vertebrae; and on each side the ribs sweep downwards and forwards, so that the front of a rib lies lower than its back. The spaces between the ribs are filled by the three layers of intercostal muscles. The cage is narrow above, where it is overlapped by the clavicles and scapulae of the shoulder girdle, and widest around the eighth and ninth ribs. Its lower border, the costal margin, is formed by the fused seventh to tenth costal cartilages and marks the edge of the abdominal wall.

sections.heading: Sternum and ribs
sections.body: OpenStax describes the sternum as three parts: the manubrium at the top, which receives the clavicles and first costal cartilages; the long body; and the small xiphoid process below, cartilaginous in youth and ossifying with age. The manubrium and body meet at the sternal angle, where the second costal cartilage attaches, and ribs three to seven join the body. Each rib ends in front in a hyaline costal cartilage. Ribs one to seven are true ribs because their cartilages reach the sternum directly; ribs eight to twelve are false ribs, with ribs eight to ten joining the cartilage of the rib above and ribs eleven and twelve, the short floating ribs, ending in the muscles of the abdominal wall. A typical rib has a head with two facets, a neck, a tubercle and a curved shaft grooved along its lower inner edge by the costal groove.

sections.heading: Joints, ligaments and movements
sections.body: Behind, the head of each typical rib (StatPearls specifies ribs two to nine) articulates with the bodies of two adjacent vertebrae and the disc between them at the costovertebral joint, while the tubercle meets the transverse process at the costotransverse joint; the first and lowest ribs meet a single vertebra. In front, the first costal cartilage is fused to the manubrium, the second to seventh form small synovial sternocostal joints, and the cartilages of ribs six to ten meet at interchondral joints. The manubriosternal joint is cartilaginous and allows slight hinging at the sternal angle. The rib rotates about the axis through its two posterior joints: the upper ribs swing the sternum forwards like a pump handle, deepening the chest from front to back, while the lower ribs flare outwards like a bucket handle, widening it. Elastic costal cartilages recoil in expiration.

sections.heading: Blood supply and nerves
sections.body: Each intercostal space is supplied from both ends: posterior intercostal arteries from the aorta meet anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery, forming a ring round the chest. StatPearls describes the intercostal vein, artery and nerve, in that order from above downwards, lying in the costal groove along the lower edge of the rib between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, with a smaller collateral bundle on the upper edge of the rib below. The nerve lies lowest, which is why it is readily reached in an intercostal nerve block, and StatPearls cautions that the bundle is not always tucked safely under the rib, particularly in older people and upper spaces, which matters when placing a chest drain. Each intercostal nerve, the anterior ramus of a thoracic spinal nerve, supplies the intercostal muscles and a strip of skin.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The cage protects the heart, lungs, great vessels, oesophagus and, under its lower ribs, the liver, spleen and kidneys. It is the engine of breathing: contraction of the diaphragm lowers the floor of the thorax, and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs through the pump-handle and bucket-handle movements described above, enlarging the chest in every direction so that air is drawn in; quiet expiration is largely elastic recoil, with the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles recruited for forced breathing and coughing. The sternum and ribs anchor the pectoral muscles, serratus anterior and the muscles of the back that move the shoulder girdle, and the ribs contain red marrow that remains active throughout life. The cartilaginous front of the cage, rather than bone, is what allows the chest to be compressed during cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Ribs break or bruise after falls, blows and road collisions. The NHS describes severe chest pain that is worse on breathing in or coughing, swelling or tenderness over the affected ribs, sometimes bruising, and a crack felt or heard at the time of injury. An X-ray is often unnecessary, because fractures may not show; when imaging is done it is to look for complications such as a pneumothorax, in which air collects around the lung and causes breathlessness and pain. Worsening breathlessness, increasing chest pain, pain in the abdomen or shoulder, or coughing up blood need emergency assessment, because lower rib fractures can injure the liver or spleen and several adjacent fractures can impair breathing. CT is used in major trauma. Pain at the costochondral junctions may arise from the joints themselves, and the sternum is a site for bone marrow sampling.

shoulder-girdle.title: Shoulder Anatomy
shoulder-girdle.descriptor: Rotator Cuff, Joints, Deltoid, Bones & Blood Supply
shoulder-girdle.intro: The shoulder is built from the clavicle and scapula, which together form the shoulder (pectoral) girdle, and the top of the humerus, which meets the scapula at the shoulder joint. Unlike the pelvic girdle it is built for mobility rather than weight-bearing: its only bony link to the axial skeleton is the small sternoclavicular joint, and the scapula otherwise floats on the back of the rib cage, held and moved by muscles. This arrangement lets the shoulder socket be positioned over a wide range so that the hand can reach almost anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Bones
keyFacts.value: Clavicle (collarbone), scapula (shoulder blade) and the upper end of the humerus (upper arm bone) on each side

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The clavicle lies horizontally across the root of the neck at the top of the chest, easily felt and seen along its whole length. Its medial end rests on the manubrium of the sternum beside the first costal cartilage; its flattened lateral end meets the acromion at the point of the shoulder. Beneath its middle third pass the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus as they cross the first rib into the axilla, so the bone acts as a strut that holds the limb away from the chest and keeps these structures clear. The scapula is a flat triangular bone lying on the posterolateral chest wall over ribs two to seven, separated from them by muscle. Its medial border runs parallel to the vertebral column, its lateral angle carries the glenoid cavity that faces forwards and outwards, and its spine crosses the back surface to end in the acromion, the bony tip of the shoulder. The head of the humerus, the top of the upper arm bone, meets the glenoid cavity of the scapula to form the shoulder joint.

sections.heading: Bones and their features
sections.body: The clavicle is an S-shaped long bone; it is the first bone to begin ossifying in the embryo and one of the last to finish, and StatPearls notes that it has a periosteal blood supply with no central nutrient artery. The scapula has two surfaces and three borders. The concave front surface, the subscapular fossa, faces the ribs; the back surface is divided by the spine into the smaller supraspinous and larger infraspinous fossae, housing the muscles of the same names, and the spine continues laterally into the broad acromion. From the upper border the hook-like coracoid process juts forwards beneath the clavicle, giving attachment to ligaments and muscles. The glenoid cavity is a shallow, pear-shaped socket deepened slightly by a fibrocartilage labrum, with small tubercles above and below for the long heads of biceps and triceps. At the top of the humerus the smooth rounded head forms the ball of the shoulder joint. The anatomical neck lies just below the head and separates it from the greater and lesser tubercles. The greater tubercle is on the outer side and the lesser tubercle at the front, and both give attachment to rotator cuff tendons. The intertubercular (bicipital) groove runs between the tubercles and holds the tendon of the long head of biceps. Below the tubercles the bone narrows at the surgical neck, where the expanded upper end meets the shaft, and fractures are common there.

sections.heading: The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint
sections.body: The shoulder, or glenohumeral, joint is a ball-and-socket synovial joint in which the rounded head of the humerus fits into the glenoid cavity of the scapula. Ball-and-socket joints have the greatest range of motion of all synovial joints. This mobility comes at a cost in stability, because the glenoid is a shallow socket and the joint capsule is loose. A rim of fibrocartilage called the glenoid labrum runs around the edge of the socket, deepening it and adding stability. Thickened bands within the capsule form the glenohumeral ligaments, which are among the static stabilisers of the joint, along with the labrum, the capsule and the shape of the bones. Muscles add dynamic stability, mainly the rotator cuff; the long head of biceps arises from the top of the glenoid and labrum, and its stabilising role is debated. The subacromial bursa lies beneath the acromion and deltoid and above the supraspinatus, which it protects from rubbing against the acromion. The rotator cuff tendons and this bursa pass through the space between the head of the humerus and the arch formed by the acromion, coracoid process and coracoacromial ligament.

sections.heading: The rotator cuff and deltoid
sections.body: The rotator cuff is made up of four muscles, the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, often remembered by the letters SITS. Their tendons blend with the joint capsule to form a cuff around the joint. Supraspinatus helps to stabilise the joint and to start abduction, lifting the arm out to the side. Infraspinatus and teres minor rotate the arm outwards, while subscapularis rotates it inwards. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus, the axillary nerve supplies teres minor, and the upper and lower subscapular nerves supply subscapularis. The deltoid arises from the lateral part of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula, and attaches to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. It has clavicular, acromial and spinal parts, is supplied by the axillary nerve, and its middle fibres abduct the arm.

sections.heading: Sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, and movement
sections.body: OpenStax describes the sternoclavicular joint as the only bony articulation between the pectoral girdle and the axial skeleton. It is a saddle-shaped synovial joint with an intra-articular disc, capsular ligaments and, most importantly, the costoclavicular ligament tying the clavicle to the first rib; it rarely dislocates, and violent force breaks the clavicle instead. The acromioclavicular joint is a plane synovial joint whose own capsular ligaments are relatively weak, so its stability comes from the coracoclavicular ligament (conoid and trapezoid parts) anchoring the coracoid process to the clavicle. Together these joints let the scapula rise and fall, protract and retract, and rotate so that the glenoid tilts upwards; raising the arm overhead draws about a third of its range from this scapular rotation, a muscular gliding on the chest wall rather than a true joint. The deltoid abducts the arm; its front fibres help flex it and its back fibres help extend it.

sections.heading: Muscles, blood supply and nerves
sections.body: The scapula is slung from the trunk by trapezius, levator scapulae and the rhomboids behind, and by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor in front; serratus anterior holds the medial border against the ribs, and when its long thoracic nerve is damaged the scapula wings away from the chest. According to StatPearls, the clavicle is supplied by branches of the suprascapular, thoracoacromial and internal thoracic arteries, and the acromioclavicular joint by the suprascapular artery (from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian) and the thoracoacromial artery (from the axillary), draining through the suprascapular vein towards the external jugular. The scapula receives the suprascapular, dorsal scapular and circumflex scapular arteries, which anastomose around the bone. Sensory nerves to the joints come from the supraclavicular, suprascapular, lateral pectoral and axillary nerves. The axillary nerve comes from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and passes through the quadrangular space beside the surgical neck of the humerus, together with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. The suprascapular nerve comes from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus and passes through the suprascapular notch. The anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries arise from the axillary artery and together supply the shoulder joint, while the suprascapular artery supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The girdle is a mobile base for the arm. Because the glenoid is shallow and the clavicle is the only bony anchor, the shoulder sacrifices stability for range: the scapula can glide round the curved chest wall to point the socket forwards, upwards or sideways, and the clavicle, pivoting at the sternoclavicular joint, keeps the shoulder a fixed distance from the midline so that the arm does not collapse onto the chest. Forces transmitted up the arm, as when pushing or falling onto an outstretched hand, pass through the glenoid and along the clavicle to the sternum, which is why that bone is the one to break. The girdle also provides the attachment and lever arms for the muscles that lift, carry and throw, and the coracoid, acromion and coracoacromial ligament form an arch over the humeral head that stops it being driven upwards. The rotator cuff muscles stabilise the joint while the deltoid lifts the arm.

sections.heading: Dislocation and fractures near the shoulder
sections.body: A dislocated shoulder means the upper arm bone has come out of its socket. The NHS advises going to A&E if the arm cannot be moved, the shoulder looks out of place or has changed shape, or it is painful, bruised or swollen. Treatment is usually a reduction in hospital, in which a clinician moves the bone back into place, followed by a sling. The axillary nerve is the nerve most often injured in shoulder dislocation, causing weak lifting of the arm to the side and loss of feeling over the outer upper arm. Most such nerve injuries recover without surgery, but numbness, pins and needles, or arm movement that is not improving should be checked: ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111, or go to A&E if it follows a new injury. A fracture of the proximal humerus, the top of the upper arm bone, causes pain, swelling and difficulty moving the arm, and bruising can spread to the chest, elbow and forearm. Many of these fractures do not need surgery, and a sling is the usual first step. A suspected fracture, especially with severe pain, needs assessment in A&E; if the arm or hand is also numb or tingling, has pins and needles, or looks pale, blue or grey or feels cold, go to A&E or call 999 straight away.

sections.heading: Rotator cuff problems, impingement and frozen shoulder
sections.body: Rotator cuff problems range from irritation of the tendons, called tendinopathy or tendinitis, to partial or full-thickness tears. Tears can develop gradually over time or suddenly, for example after a fall. Rotator cuff tears can cause pain and weakness when lifting the arm, and night pain is common. Most people start with non-surgical care such as physiotherapy, and surgery is considered for some tears. Sudden arm weakness after an injury needs prompt medical assessment: go to A&E if the arm cannot be moved or the shoulder looks out of shape, or ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111; call 999 if there is also a drooping face or slurred speech, which can be signs of a stroke. Shoulder impingement is pain that arises when the rotator cuff tendons and subacromial bursa are compressed beneath the arch above the humeral head, and it typically hurts when the arm is lifted forwards or sideways. In frozen shoulder the joint capsule tightens and becomes inflamed, causing pain and stiffness, often with night pain. The cause is often unclear, but it is linked to diabetes, thyroid disorders and previous shoulder injury or surgery. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if shoulder pain does not improve.

sections.heading: Collarbone and acromioclavicular injuries
sections.body: The clavicle is one of the most often fractured bones, usually after a fall onto the shoulder or outstretched hand. NHS emergency department leaflets describe pain, swelling and bruising over the bone, a palpable step and a drooping shoulder; numbness or tingling in the arm is uncommon but needs prompt attention. The diagnosis is confirmed on X-ray, and most fractures heal in a sling with simple painkillers, often leaving a lump; surgery is reserved for severe injuries such as bone breaking the skin or badly displaced fragments. Bone through the skin, a changed shoulder shape, heavy bleeding or difficulty breathing need emergency assessment. Acromioclavicular dislocations follow falls onto the point of the shoulder and are graded on X-ray by how far the clavicle rides up as the coracoclavicular ligament tears. Scapular fractures are rare, imply major trauma and usually prompt chest CT.

spleen.title: Spleen Anatomy
spleen.descriptor: Position, Ligaments, Splenic Vessels, Red and White Pulp & Function
spleen.intro: The spleen is a soft, highly vascular organ in the left upper abdomen, tucked beneath the diaphragm behind the stomach and protected by the lower ribs. It is the largest lymphoid organ in the body: its red pulp filters the blood and removes old or damaged red cells, while its white pulp houses the lymphocytes that mount adaptive immune responses to blood-borne antigens.

keyFacts.value: Left hypochondrium, between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm, under cover of the ninth to eleventh ribs

keyFacts.label: Hilum
keyFacts.value: On the visceral surface; transmits the splenic vessels and nerves and gives attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Splenic artery from the coeliac trunk, running along the upper border of the pancreas within the splenorenal ligament

keyFacts.label: Venous drainage
keyFacts.value: Splenic vein, passing behind the pancreas to join the superior mesenteric vein and form the portal vein

keyFacts.label: Tissue
keyFacts.value: Red pulp (filters blood, recycles red cells) and white pulp (B-cell germinal centres with surrounding T cells around a central arteriole)

keyFacts.label: Variation
keyFacts.value: Accessory spleens are common and most often lie at the hilum

keyFacts.label: Clinical
keyFacts.value: Enlargement in liver disease and blood disorders; rupture after trauma; lifelong infection risk after splenectomy

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium, high under the dome of the left diaphragm, with its long axis following the line of the tenth rib. Its smooth diaphragmatic surface is convex and faces upwards and backwards towards the diaphragm, which separates it from the pleura, the lung and the ninth, tenth and eleventh ribs. The visceral surface is moulded by its neighbours: the fundus of the stomach in front, the left kidney behind, the splenic flexure of the colon below, and the tail of the pancreas, which reaches the hilum. Because it is entirely hidden by the ribs, a normal spleen cannot be felt; it only becomes palpable below the left costal margin once it has enlarged considerably, and it then moves downwards and medially with breathing.

sections.heading: Ligaments and hilum
sections.body: The spleen is covered by peritoneum except at the hilum, a fissure on the visceral surface that transmits the splenic vessels and nerves and provides attachment for two peritoneal folds. The gastrosplenic ligament runs forward to the greater curvature of the stomach and carries the short gastric and left gastro-epiploic vessels, while the splenorenal ligament runs backwards to the left kidney and contains the splenic artery and vein together with the tail of the pancreas. These ligaments suspend the spleen within the greater sac and form the left boundary of the lesser sac behind the stomach. A wandering or displaced spleen can result from laxity of these supporting ligaments, allowing the organ to drift on a long vascular pedicle that may twist and cut off its blood supply.

sections.heading: Blood supply and innervation
sections.body: The splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk, takes a tortuous course laterally across the superior aspect of the pancreas, enters the splenorenal ligament and divides into several branches near the hilum, each supplying a distinct region of the organ; these segments have little overlap, which is why partial removal of the spleen is possible. The splenic vein emerges from the hilum, passes behind the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein, so splenic blood reaches the liver before the general circulation. Lymph drains along the splenic vessels to nodes at the hilum and along the pancreas, then to the coeliac nodes. The nerve supply is sympathetic, from the coeliac plexus, travelling with the artery and controlling the tone of the capsule and vessels.

sections.heading: Structure and function
sections.body: Beneath a thin capsule the spleen is divided by trabeculae into splenic nodules, each containing red pulp and white pulp. Red pulp consists mostly of red blood cells held in a network of reticular fibres with fixed and free macrophages and all the other cell types found in blood, including some lymphocytes. White pulp resembles the lymphoid follicles of a lymph node: it surrounds a central arteriole and consists of germinal centres of dividing B cells surrounded by T cells and accessory cells. The red pulp mainly filters the blood using relatively non-specific immune cells, removing injured and old red blood cells and recycling their iron, while the white pulp is where adaptive T-cell and B-cell responses to blood-borne antigens take place. The spleen also acts as a reservoir of platelets and monocytes.

sections.heading: Variation
sections.body: Accessory spleens, small nodules of splenic tissue separate from the main organ, are a common finding and most often lie at the splenic hilum where the splenic vessels enter and leave; they may also be found in the gastrosplenic ligament, the tail of the pancreas or the greater omentum. They matter clinically because an accessory spleen left behind at splenectomy can continue to destroy blood cells in conditions where the operation was done to stop that, and because on imaging a nodule near the pancreatic tail can be mistaken for a tumour. The notches on the superior border of the spleen are remnants of the lobulated form it has in the embryo, when it develops from mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium. The number of hilar arterial branches also varies between individuals.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: An enlarged spleen is usually a sign of another condition, such as cirrhosis, leukaemia or rheumatoid arthritis, and is managed by treating the cause rather than by removal; people with an enlarged spleen are advised to avoid contact sports because the organ is more likely to rupture. Rupture can follow blunt trauma to the left lower ribs, and because the organ is so vascular it bleeds heavily into the peritoneal cavity; a painful spleen may signal damage, rupture or enlargement. Where possible the spleen is now preserved and the bleeding controlled, because removal carries a lifelong risk that a serious infection may develop quickly. People without a spleen are offered vaccinations, ideally before the operation, and some take long-term antibiotics. The spleen is assessed by palpation, ultrasound and CT; blood films showing Howell-Jolly bodies indicate loss of splenic function.

thymus.title: Thymus Anatomy
thymus.descriptor: Lobes, Mediastinal Position, Blood Supply & T-cell Maturation
thymus.intro: The thymus is a soft, two-lobed lymphoid organ lying behind the upper sternum in the superior and anterior mediastinum, in front of the great vessels and the heart. It is the primary lymphoid organ in which T lymphocytes mature: immature cells arriving from the bone marrow are tested against the body's own tissues and most are destroyed, so that only cells able to recognise foreign antigen without attacking self are released. The gland is largest in childhood and is gradually replaced by fat with age.

keyFacts.value: Superior and anterior mediastinum, behind the manubrium, in front of the great vessels and pericardium; the upper poles may reach the thyroid

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Right and left lobes, each with an outer cortex and inner medulla; the lobes keep separate vessels, lymphatics and nerves

keyFacts.value: Primary lymphoid organ (with the bone marrow)

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Branches of the inferior thyroid and internal thoracic arteries, with smaller contributions from the pericardiacophrenic and anterior intercostal arteries

keyFacts.label: Venous drainage
keyFacts.value: Thymic veins to the left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein

keyFacts.label: Development
keyFacts.value: Two lobes form from the sixth week of gestation and fuse in the anterosuperior mediastinum around the eighth week

keyFacts.label: Imaging
