sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The thymus lies in the superior part of the retrosternal mediastinum, immediately behind the manubrium and the upper part of the body of the sternum, and extends down into the anterior mediastinum in front of the pericardium. Behind it lie the left brachiocephalic vein, the arch of the aorta and its branches, and the trachea; on each side are the pleurae and the phrenic nerves. In children the upper poles of the two lobes often reach up through the thoracic inlet into the neck as far as the lower edge of the thyroid, following the gland's embryological path of descent. StatPearls notes that variation in the number, size and position of the lobes is common, and accessory thymic tissue may be found anywhere along the line of descent from the pharynx to the mediastinum.

sections.heading: Lobes and structure
sections.body: The thymus is bilobed, and the two lobes, though pressed together and joined by connective tissue, keep separate blood supplies, lymphatic drainage and innervation throughout life. Each lobe is enclosed in a capsule whose septa divide it into lobules. OpenStax describes a densely packed outer cortex, which stains intensely because it is crowded with developing lymphocytes, and a paler inner medulla, where the surviving thymocytes gather before leaving the organ. The framework of both zones is a network of epithelial cells, with macrophages and dendritic cells among them; the medulla also contains whorled Hassall's corpuscles of keratinised epithelium that are characteristic of the thymus under the microscope. Tight capillary walls and an epithelial sheath form a blood-thymus barrier in the cortex that shields developing cells from circulating antigens.

sections.heading: Blood supply, drainage and nerves
sections.body: The thymus has no single named artery. StatPearls describes its blood as coming mainly from the inferior thyroid arteries above and branches of the internal thoracic (internal mammary) arteries on each side, whose lateral branches to the gland are sometimes called the lateral thymic arteries, with minor contributions from the pericardiacophrenic and anterior intercostal arteries. The veins follow the arteries, and a large posterior thymic vein drains into the left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein that passes directly behind the gland; this vein is at risk during surgery on the thymus. Lymph leaves through the parasternal, brachiocephalic and tracheobronchial nodes; the thymus has no afferent lymphatics, which fits its role as a site of lymphocyte production rather than antigen filtering. Its sympathetic and vagal nerve supply is small and reaches it with the vessels.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: OpenStax identifies the bone marrow and thymus as the two primary lymphoid organs. B lymphocytes complete their development in the marrow, but immature T cells, the thymocytes, leave the marrow and migrate to the thymus to mature. In the cortex they meet cortical epithelial cells and are tested: those that cannot recognise the body's own MHC molecules, and those that bind self-antigens too strongly, are eliminated, so that only a small fraction of the cells that enter leave as mature, functional T cells. Survivors emerge as single-positive cells carrying either CD4 or CD8 and pass through the medulla into the blood to populate the lymph nodes and spleen. The process teaches T cells to recognise foreign antigen presented on self-MHC while remaining tolerant of self. Thymic epithelial cells also secrete hormones such as thymosin that support this maturation.

sections.heading: Development and involution
sections.body: The thymus develops from the third pharyngeal pouches on each side; the two primordia begin to form around the sixth week of gestation, descend into the chest and fuse in the anterosuperior mediastinum around the eighth week, which is why the lobes remain functionally separate. Lymphoid precursors from the bone marrow colonise the epithelial framework and the gland is already active before birth. Relative to body size it is largest in infancy and reaches its greatest absolute weight around puberty, after which it involutes: lymphoid tissue is slowly replaced by fat so that the adult thymus is a fatty remnant that still produces a trickle of new T cells. Because of this, the thymus is easy to see on a child's chest radiograph but is usually inconspicuous in adults, and a prominent mediastinal mass in an adult is treated as abnormal.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Thymoma, a tumour of the thymic epithelium, is the commonest tumour of the anterior mediastinum in adults and frequently occurs together with myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction. The NHS describes weakness of the eye, eyelid, facial, chewing and swallowing muscles that worsens after activity and improves with rest. Investigation includes blood tests for the responsible antibodies, nerve conduction studies and, for the thymus itself, a CT or MRI scan of the chest to check whether the gland is larger than usual or contains a tumour. Removal of the thymus (thymectomy) is part of the treatment for thymoma and for some people with myasthenia. Failure of the thymus to develop, as in DiGeorge syndrome, leaves a child without T cells and prone to severe infections, and a large normal thymus in an infant is a common cause of a widened mediastinum on X-ray.

ureters.title: Ureter Anatomy
ureters.descriptor: Course, Constrictions, Blood Supply & Urine Transport
ureters.intro: The ureters are a pair of muscular tubes that carry urine from the renal pelvis of each kidney down the posterior abdominal wall and across the pelvis to the trigone of the bladder. Urine does not simply drain by gravity: waves of peristalsis in the ureteric wall propel it towards the bladder, and the oblique entry of each ureter through the bladder wall acts as a valve that stops urine flowing back.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Retroperitoneal throughout, from the hilum of the kidney to the base of the bladder

keyFacts.label: Length
keyFacts.value: Approximately 30 cm in the adult

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Abdominal and pelvic portions, meeting at the pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery

keyFacts.label: Narrowings
keyFacts.value: Pelviureteric junction, the crossing of the pelvic brim, and the vesicoureteric junction

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Segmental: renal, gonadal, aortic and common iliac branches above; vesical and other internal iliac branches below

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: Transitional epithelium, longitudinal and circular smooth muscle, and an adventitia carrying the vessels

keyFacts.label: Function
keyFacts.value: Peristaltic transport of urine from kidney to bladder

sections.heading: Location and course
sections.body: Each ureter begins at the pelviureteric junction, roughly at the level of the second lumbar vertebra, where the renal pelvis funnels down and narrows into the ureter. From the apex of the renal pelvis at the kidney hilum the ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle, remaining retroperitoneal throughout its abdominal course, and crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, where it enters the pelvis. It then runs down the lateral pelvic wall, lying on the internal iliac artery, before turning forwards and medially to pierce the posterolateral wall of the bladder. The two ureters open into the bladder at the upper corners of the trigone. On an abdominal radiograph the ureter follows the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, a useful guide when looking for stones.

sections.heading: Parts and relations
sections.body: The ureter is divided into abdominal and pelvic portions at the pelvic brim. In the abdomen it is crossed anteriorly by the gonadal vessels and, on the right, lies behind the second part of the duodenum and the vessels of the right colon, while on the left it passes behind the left colic vessels and the sigmoid mesocolon. In the pelvis its relations differ between the sexes. In the female the ureter runs beneath the uterine artery close to the cervix, so it is at risk when the artery is tied during hysterectomy; in the male the vas deferens crosses above it just before it reaches the bladder. The ureter is narrowest at three points: the pelviureteric junction, the crossing of the pelvic brim and the vesicoureteric junction, where it passes obliquely through the bladder wall. These are the sites where stones lodge.

sections.heading: Blood supply and innervation
sections.body: The arterial supply is segmental. The abdominal ureter receives branches from the renal, gonadal and common iliac arteries and directly from the abdominal aorta; the pelvic ureter is supplied by branches of the internal iliac artery, including the vesical and, in the female, uterine arteries. These vessels run along the ureter within its outer coat and join to form an anastomotic plexus, so the ureter can survive division of one or two feeders, but it cannot be stripped or resected proximally and distally at the same time without compromising its blood supply. Veins follow the arteries, and lymph drains to the lumbar and iliac nodes. The ureter is supplied by autonomic fibres from the renal, aortic and hypogastric plexuses; its pain fibres return to the lower thoracic and upper lumbar segments, which is why ureteric colic is felt in the loin and radiates to the groin.

sections.heading: Structure and function
sections.body: The ureteric wall has three layers: a mucosa of transitional epithelium that can stretch without tearing, a thick muscular coat of longitudinal and circular smooth muscle, and an outer adventitia that carries the vessels and nerves. Urine does not passively drain into the bladder but is propelled by waves of peristalsis that begin in the smooth muscle of the renal pelvis and travel down the ureter, each wave pushing a bolus of urine ahead of a contraction that almost closes the lumen. The oblique passage of the ureter through the bladder wall means that as the bladder fills and its wall tightens, the intramural ureter is compressed, forming a valve that prevents urine refluxing towards the kidney. Peristaltic frequency rises when urine production increases, and at very high flows the ureter can remain open and conduct urine as a continuous column.

sections.heading: Variation
sections.body: Because the ureter develops from the ureteric bud, an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct that grows towards the metanephric kidney, early branching of the bud produces a duplicated system: two ureters may drain one kidney, joining before the bladder or opening separately, in which case the upper-pole ureter opens lower and more medially than expected. A ureter that fails to join the bladder properly opens ectopically into the urethra or genital tract. A retrocaval ureter passes behind the inferior vena cava and may be compressed by it. Where the kidney itself is abnormal, as in a horseshoe kidney, the ureters pass in front of the fused isthmus and may be kinked. Congenital narrowing at the pelviureteric junction or incompetence of the vesicoureteric valve, allowing reflux of infected urine, are both recognised causes of kidney damage in childhood.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Stones are the commonest ureteric problem. Many cause no symptoms while in the kidney, but when a stone moves into the ureter it stretches the tube and causes renal colic, a severe cramping pain in the flank that comes and goes and may travel to the groin; blood in the urine is common. A stone blocking the ureter can lead to kidney infection, and fever is a warning sign that requires urgent treatment. Non-contrast CT is the standard first test, with ultrasound preferred in pregnancy and in children; blood tests check kidney function and signs of infection. Small stones often pass on their own, while stones that do not may be removed or fragmented through a thin telescope passed up the ureter (ureteroscopy). The ureter is also at risk of injury in pelvic surgery, particularly where it crosses deep to the uterine artery, and of compression by tumours or fibrosis.

uterine-ligaments.title: Uterine Ligaments Anatomy
uterine-ligaments.descriptor: Broad, Round, Cardinal, Uterosacral & Ovarian Ligaments
uterine-ligaments.intro: The uterus, uterine tubes and ovaries are held in the pelvis by a set of peritoneal folds and fibromuscular bands rather than by any bony attachment. The broad ligament drapes over the uterus like a sheet, the round ligaments pull the uterus forwards, and the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments anchor the cervix to the pelvic side walls and sacrum. Together with the pelvic floor muscles they keep the pelvic organs in position; when they weaken, the organs descend and prolapse into the vagina.

keyFacts.label: Broad ligament
keyFacts.value: Double fold of peritoneum from the sides of the uterus to the pelvic side walls; subdivided into mesometrium, mesosalpinx and mesovarium

keyFacts.label: Round ligament
keyFacts.value: Fibromuscular band from the uterine cornu through the inguinal canal to the labium majus; remnant of the gubernaculum

keyFacts.label: Cardinal ligament
keyFacts.value: Thickened pelvic fascia at the base of the broad ligament, from cervix and vaginal fornix to the pelvic side wall; carries the uterine artery

keyFacts.label: Uterosacral ligament
keyFacts.value: From the cervix backwards, beneath the peritoneum, to the front of the sacrum

keyFacts.label: Ovarian ligament
keyFacts.value: Joins the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus below the uterine tube

keyFacts.label: Suspensory ligament of the ovary
keyFacts.value: Peritoneal fold carrying the ovarian vessels from the ovary to the lateral abdominal wall

keyFacts.label: Vesico-uterine pouch
keyFacts.value: Peritoneal recess between the bladder and the front of the uterus

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The uterus lies in the true pelvis between the bladder in front and the rectum behind, and in most women it is tilted forwards (anteverted) over the bladder and bent forwards on itself (anteflexed). Peritoneum covers its upper surface and runs off it on either side as the broad ligament, which reaches the lateral pelvic wall. In front, the peritoneum dips between the bladder and uterus to form the shallow vesico-uterine pouch; behind, it drops much lower between the uterus and rectum to form the recto-uterine pouch. Beneath the peritoneum, the condensed pelvic fascia around the cervix (the parametrium) thickens into the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments, which are the true load-bearing supports of the cervix and upper vagina.

sections.heading: The broad ligament and its parts
sections.body: The broad ligament is a double sheet of peritoneum draped over the uterus and uterine tubes, connecting them to the pelvic side walls and floor. Its largest part, the mesometrium, hangs from the body of the uterus; the mesosalpinx is the narrow upper fold enclosing the uterine tube; and the mesovarium is the short fold that suspends the ovary from its posterior surface. Between the two peritoneal layers run the uterine tube, the round and ovarian ligaments, the uterine and ovarian vessels, lymphatics, nerves and, near the cervix, the ureter. StatPearls describes the broad ligament as giving only secondary support: it keeps the organs in their relative positions but does not itself hold the uterus up.

sections.heading: Round, ovarian and suspensory ligaments
sections.body: The round ligament is a cord of fibromuscular tissue that leaves the uterus at the cornu, just in front of the uterine tube, runs forwards in the broad ligament, passes through the inguinal canal and fades into the labium majus. It is a remnant of the fetal gubernaculum and helps to keep the uterus anteverted and anteflexed; it carries small vessels, lymphatics and nerves. The ovarian ligament is the other half of the same embryological cord, running from the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus behind the tube. The suspensory ligament of the ovary is not a ligament in the fibrous sense but a fold of peritoneum that conveys the ovarian artery, vein, lymphatics and nerves from the lateral abdominal wall to the ovary, continuous with the mesovarium.

sections.heading: Cardinal and uterosacral ligaments
sections.body: The paired cardinal (transverse cervical or Mackenrodt's) ligaments form the lower edge of the broad ligament. Each is a thickening of parametrium and pelvic fascia extending from the cervix and vaginal fornix medially to the lateral pelvic wall, and it provides lateral support for the cervix. The uterine artery travels within the cardinal ligament on its way from the internal iliac artery to the uterus, crossing above the ureter close to the cervix, which is why the ureter is at risk during hysterectomy. The uterosacral ligaments run from the back of the cervix, beneath the peritoneum, to the front of the sacrum on each side of the rectum, resisting forward and downward displacement. StatPearls describes the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments together as the apical support of the uterus and vaginal vault.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The ligaments share the work of support with the levator ani muscles of the pelvic floor, on which the pelvic organs normally rest. The cardinal-uterosacral complex suspends the cervix and upper vagina over the levator plate; the round ligaments steer the uterus forwards so that intra-abdominal pressure presses it onto the bladder rather than down the vagina; and the broad ligament keeps the tubes and ovaries in a position from which a released egg can be caught by the fimbriae. The fibromuscular ligaments are not rigid: they stretch during pregnancy as the uterus rises out of the pelvis, and the round ligaments in particular can be a source of sharp lower abdominal pain in later pregnancy as they are pulled taut.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Weakening of the pelvic floor muscles and supporting ligaments allows the uterus, bladder or bowel to bulge into the vagina: pelvic organ prolapse. The NHS lists pregnancy and childbirth (particularly a large baby, an assisted delivery or a long labour), being overweight, chronic constipation or coughing, previous pelvic surgery such as hysterectomy, the menopause and a family history as factors that make it more likely. Women describe heaviness or something coming down, often eased by lying flat, and may have bladder or bowel symptoms. Diagnosis is clinical: the NHS describes an examination that feels the pelvis for lumps and uses a speculum to look at the vaginal walls, which also grades the prolapse. Surgery for apical prolapse often uses the uterosacral or sacrospinous ligaments to re-suspend the vaginal vault, and the round ligament is a common source of pain in pregnancy.
